A breaker for direct current, which offers no zero crossing to help it. It has to force the current to zero itself — with a resonant circuit or with semiconductors — which is why DC breakers arrived decades after AC ones and still cost far more.

A plant design in which the array and the battery share a direct-current bus behind a single inverter, usually through a DC/DC converter. Avoids one conversion step and can capture energy the inverter would otherwise clip, at the cost of a more tightly coupled design.

A converter that changes one DC voltage to another without passing through AC. It is the stage that does the work once power has arrived as direct current — inside a rack, inside a vehicle, or on a server board — and it is what lets a high-voltage DC bus feed low-voltage electronics.

The direct-current stage inside a static UPS between the rectifier and the inverter, where the battery connects. Every watt the load draws in double conversion passes through it as DC, which is why the batteries can take over without any switching event — they are already on the bus.

Data centre infrastructure management: software that inventories the physical plant — racks, circuits, cooling units, sensors — and monitors it as one live system. Its practical purpose is capacity planning: finding the power, cooling, space and redundancy that have been paid for and cannot currently be used.

Distribution cost recovery factor: a Texas rider that lets a wires utility recover new distribution investment between base rate cases, filed annually against a statutory formula. With interim transmission updates it is the reason a Texas TDU's earnings track its capital plan with only months of lag rather than years.

A generator's formal notice to its grid operator that it intends to stop running a unit. The operator studies whether the system can live without it, and may require it to keep running under a reliability agreement until replacement wires or generation arrive.

A deliberate pause in which both switches of a half-bridge are off, inserted so they can never be on together across the supply. Too little risks a destructive shoot-through; too much forces current through a body diode and wastes energy.

The heat a reactor keeps producing after the chain reaction stops, from the radioactive decay of fission products — roughly 6-7% of full power at shutdown, falling over hours and days. Removing it is the central safety problem of every reactor.

Removing a plant at the end of its life — safely discharging and extracting equipment, restoring the site, and disposing of or recycling what comes out. It is a real cost that has to sit with someone, and lenders increasingly require that it be reserved for rather than offset against an uncertain future scrap value.
The short length of pipe joining the primary and secondary loops of a chilled-water plant. Which way water flows through it, and how much, is the plant's most useful single diagnostic.

A rate mechanism that separates a utility's revenue from the volume of energy it sells, so that selling less does not cut its earnings and selling more does not raise them — with a true-up each year. It removes the utility's incentive to oppose efficiency, and it changes what data-center load growth is worth to it: under full decoupling the growth pays for wires, not profit.

The first slice of each loss that the insured bears before the policy pays, set as a fixed amount or a percentage of insured value. Catastrophe perils such as hail often carry percentage deductibles large enough to matter to a lender.
Piles or drilled shafts that carry load past unsuitable near-surface soil to competent material below. They are chosen when the ground near the surface cannot be made good enough.

The rate at which defective units escape a manufacturing process and reach the customer, expressed per million produced. At storage scale it is decisive: an enclosure holds thousands of cells, so a rate that sounds excellent still puts defective cells into ordinary projects.

An explosion caused by flammable gas accumulating in an enclosed space and igniting — a distinct hazard from fire itself. In battery enclosures it is controlled by stopping the accumulation, through ventilation or inert gas, or by giving the pressure a deliberate escape route.
The gradual loss of a battery's usable capacity with cycling and age. Storage contracts manage it with capacity guarantees and planned augmentation.

The value of the battery life consumed by one charge-discharge cycle, expressed as money per megawatt-hour moved. A dispatch decision is only profitable if the price spread captured exceeds this cost plus round-trip losses, which is why an optimizer will decline spreads that look positive on the price screen alone.

Construction-phase insurance for the revenue a project loses if an insured event delays commissioning past the date the financing assumed — the builder's-risk counterpart of business-interruption cover.

A loan that is committed up front but drawn in tranches as the borrower needs cash — typically as equipment is ordered or construction milestones are hit. Common for GPU fleets and data-center builds, where spending is staged.

The small fraction of fission neutrons (under one percent) emitted seconds to minutes after the split rather than instantly. They are the reason a reactor responds on a human timescale and can be controlled at all.

A carrier's grant to an agent — a managing general agent or a Lloyd's coverholder — of the power to quote, bind and often adjust claims on the carrier's paper, inside limits and rules the carrier sets. The agent underwrites; the carrier holds the risk.

A landlord's headline capacity figure that adds operating buildings to everything not yet built — contracted, reserved or bare land — without saying how much of each. Useful only once the rung and the owner of each megawatt are known.

The chance that contracted capacity arrives later than the date the buyer planned around. For a compute buyer whose demand is growing, a late site means rationing customers; for the lender, a delayed backstop.

A dated point at which contracted capacity must be energized and handed over. Rent, guarantees and investor money are often tied to milestones — a missed one can delay a backstop, trigger a termination right or hold back funding.

The temperature difference between the water returning to a chiller and the water leaving it. A plant is designed around a delta-T, and the flow it must pump for a given duty is inversely proportional to it.

The part of a large customer's bill priced per kilowatt of peak demand rather than per kilowatt-hour of energy used. It pays for the wires and plant that have to exist to serve the customer's maximum draw, whether or not that draw occurs often — which is why a data center's bill is mostly demand, not energy.

A program that pays a customer to cut its grid draw when the system is stressed — by shedding load or by switching to on-site generation. Running backup engines for it moves them out of the emergency-only class, which is why the permit, not the machine, decides whether a data center can join.

Money a large electricity consumer earns for agreeing to switch off when the grid is short. For a flexible load like a mining fleet this can be worth more than the output forgone, which turns curtailment from a cost into a product.

How much of a battery's stored energy is drawn out before recharging, as a percentage of capacity. Shallower cycling generally extends cycle life, so a quoted cycle count is only meaningful alongside the depth of discharge it was measured at.

Operating equipment below its nameplate rating because real conditions — ambient temperature, altitude, state of charge, or age — do not match the conditions the rating assumed. A specification read as a guaranteed operating number rather than a rated one is one of the most common sources of a capacity shortfall that presents as an equipment fault.

An arrangement in which the builder or a specialist trade contributes to the design before it is finished, without taking design liability. It is how constructability and long-lead equipment choices get settled early on schedule-driven projects.

The party contractually entitled to approve a change to the product — a component substitution, a layout revision, a supplier swap. Confusion about who holds it is the most common cause of a manufacturing dispute.
A delivery method in which one entity holds both the design and the construction contracts, so the owner has a single point of responsibility and the two disciplines cannot blame each other.

Regulatory approval of a standardised reactor design, once, independent of any site — so that later applicants reference the approved design instead of re-litigating it. Approving the design and licensing the site are two different clocks.

The years between a component being chosen for a product and that product shipping in volume. In power semiconductors it means today's revenue was decided by decisions taken two or three years ago, and today's decisions will not show up in revenue for as long again.

The life a battery is designed to reach under ideal float conditions, quoted in years. It is not the life it will get: temperature, cycling and ripple decide the service life, which is routinely a fraction of the design figure.

Being selected as the supplier for a component in a product that is about to be built — decided during the customer's design phase, often years before volume revenue. Once designed in, a part is expensive to replace, so the win locks in the socket for that product's life.

A developer that keeps the projects it builds and earns the operating cash flow for decades. Needs long-term capital and an operations team; the reward is the whole life of the asset rather than one sale.

A developer that carries a project through permits, interconnection and contracts, then sells it to an owner before or at construction. Capital-light and quick; the price depends on which development stage the project has reached.

The difference between what a developer spent to bring a project to a saleable stage and the price a buyer pays for it — the profit on origination. It is earned on sale, not on operation, and is rarely disclosed.

Every project a developer is working on that is not yet built, from a land option to a permitted, contracted site awaiting financing. Rankings by pipeline megawatts measure ambition and options, not operating capacity.

The gap between the yield on cost of building a data centre and the cap rate a finished one sells for. That gap is the developer's profit for taking construction and leasing risk, and it is why building can be worth more than buying.

The sequence a project climbs from idea to operation: site control, interconnection request, permits, offtake, notice to proceed, financial close, construction, commercial operation. Each rung retires a risk, so each rung raises what a buyer will pay.

The temperature at which the room's air begins to condense water on a surface. Coolant supplied below it sweats every hose and cold plate onto the boards beneath, so a CDU holds its supply temperature above the data hall's dew point — one reason warm-water cooling is safer than cold.

Diesel exhaust fluid: the urea-and-water solution injected into the exhaust ahead of an SCR catalyst, where it converts nitrogen oxides into nitrogen and water. A Tier 4 engine cannot meet its emissions limit without it, so DEF supply and freeze protection become part of the site's operating plan.

A filter in the exhaust that traps soot and is periodically burned clean. Together with SCR it is the after-treatment that separates a Tier 4 engine from a Tier 2 one, and it adds backpressure, heat and maintenance the standby duty cycle does not otherwise need.

A contract clause allocating the risk of ground that turns out not to match the investigation — either differing materially from what the documents indicated, or unusual against what would ordinarily be expected. Its commercial purpose is to make bids cheaper: without it every contractor must price unknown ground pessimistically on every job.

The recalculation of network difficulty that happens every 2,016 blocks — about every two weeks. It is the mechanism that turns every rival's new machine into a direct cut in your own revenue, without any price moving.

A blockchain-recorded claim of value — a cryptocurrency, a token, or a tokenised version of a conventional asset. Regulators differ on whether particular ones are securities, commodities or something else, which is the source of most of the sector's legal uncertainty.

A simulated copy of a real asset, fed by its live data, used to rehearse changes before they touch the hardware — testing a control strategy, forecasting degradation, or learning what normal looks like so anomalies stand out. It is how an operator tries something on a plant without trying it on the plant.

A data-center lease signed by the end user itself, in its own name, rather than by a cloud provider or intermediary on its behalf. It gives the user control of the site and puts the user's own credit behind the rent.

Cooling servers by circulating liquid through cold plates bolted onto the processors, memory and other hot parts, instead of blowing air over them. Single-phase DLC keeps the fluid liquid throughout; the heat leaves the rack in a coolant loop and is handed to the building at a coolant distribution unit.
The final treatment step that inactivates pathogens — chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light. Which method is used changes what residual protection the water carries downstream.

The grid operator's instruction telling each resource how much to produce in the next interval, issued to keep supply matched to demand at least cost. A plant that is available but not dispatched earns nothing from energy that interval.

Who decides when a battery charges and discharges. Under a toll or service agreement the buyer holds them; under a merchant model the owner does — and the holder of dispatch rights holds most of the revenue risk.

Generation that can be turned on, up, down or off when the grid operator asks — gas, nuclear, hydro, and storage for as long as its energy lasts — as opposed to output that follows the weather. A plan that must serve a data center's flat load at night still buys dispatchable capacity, which is why gas keeps appearing in resource plans written under clean-energy mandates.

An asset manager's own measure of cash profit available to pay out to shareholders — fee-related earnings plus realised performance income and investment gains, less cash costs. It is not a standard accounting measure, so two managers can define it slightly differently.

ERCOT's registration class for a generator or battery connected to a distribution system rather than the transmission grid — typically under 10 MW. It follows a lighter interconnection path than a transmission-connected resource, which is why developers size projects at 9.9 MW.

UPS topologies that reach N+1 or better without doubling everything. In a block-redundant or catcher design a spare UPS system stands ready to take any block's load through static transfer switches; in a distributed-redundant design each load is fed from two of several systems so any one can fail. Both cost less than 2N, and both place the redundancy in a switching event that has to work.

In ERCOT, the company that owns the local distribution network a small generator connects to — Oncor, CenterPoint, AEP Texas, TNMP. A distribution-connected battery's interconnection is negotiated with the DSP, not with ERCOT's transmission planners.

The ratio between the sum of a facility's individual maximum demands and the maximum demand of the whole facility, which is always lower because loads do not all peak together. It is the number that lets a designer buy less generation than the nameplate sum of everything connected — and the number an AI training hall attacks, because thousands of accelerators can peak in step.

Dry low-NOx combustion: premixing fuel and air before the flame so the mixture burns lean and cool enough to form little nitrogen oxide, without injecting water or steam to do it. Lean premixed flames sit close to blowing out and close to travelling back up the burner, so the combustor is the part of a gas turbine most constrained by the fuel it is asked to burn.

A communication protocol built for electric utility networks and designed to work over unreliable links, with time-stamped reporting so a device can tell a control centre what happened while the connection was down. Common between substations, plant controllers and utility control rooms.

A commission's case file: a numbered proceeding holding the application, testimony, discovery, intervenor filings, hearing transcripts and the final order. For a seller the docket is the only place a utility's plans are stated under oath with dates attached — read the docket, not the press release.

An extra 10 percentage points of US investment or production tax credit for a project whose steel, iron and manufactured components meet a US-made threshold; the reason buyers reserve US-made batteries and modules years ahead.

The UPS mode in which all power is rectified to DC and re-made as AC by the inverter, continuously, so the load always sees a synthesized waveform and never the raw supply. It is the highest grade of protection — VFI in the IEC classification — and costs a few percent of every megawatt-hour as conversion heat; eco-mode is the alternative that idles the conversion and accepts a transfer.

A circuit breaker that racks in and out of its cell on rails, with three defined positions: connected, test (control power live, main contacts isolated) and disconnected. It lets a breaker be tested or replaced without de-energizing the bus behind it, which is why medium-voltage switchgear is built this way and why racking is one of the highest-exposure tasks in an electrical room.

A single release of loan money to a project during construction, made against a certificate that the work it pays for has been done. The independent engineer's monthly construction-monitoring report is what the lender relies on before signing each one.
Liquid water carried out of a cooling tower as droplets in the exhaust air, as distinct from water that has evaporated. It is small, it is regulated, and it carries whatever is in the basin with it.

The lightly doped layer inside a power transistor that absorbs the voltage when the device is off. It has to be thicker for a higher voltage rating, and every micron of thickness adds resistance when the device is on — the trade at the heart of power-device design.

A governor setting that lets an engine's speed fall slightly as its load rises, so several engines sharing a bus each take a predictable share of the load instead of fighting over it. Its partner is isochronous control, which holds speed exactly constant and is given to one machine or to the paralleling controller so the bus frequency stays put.

The sale of a completed project from a private sponsor to the listed vehicle it controls. Because both sides share an owner, the price is set by negotiation rather than an auction, and independent directors are usually the only check on it.

Diesel rotary uninterruptible power supply: a rotary UPS whose flywheel and synchronous machine share a shaft line with a diesel engine through a clutch. When the supply fails the flywheel carries the load for the seconds the engine needs to start and clutch in, so one machine does the work of UPS, transfer switch and generator — with no battery and no separate transfer.
Air temperature as an ordinary thermometer reads it. An air-cooled machine rejects heat against this, which is why it is less efficient than a tower on the same day.
A closed-loop finned coil that rejects heat from a fluid straight to ambient air, with no evaporation and no water. It trades efficiency and hot-day capacity for using no water at all.
Money investors have committed to a fund that the manager has not yet invested. It earns no fee in most structures until it is deployed, so a large balance is both a war chest and a drag.

A production area held at extremely low humidity because the materials inside a battery cell react with water. Cell assembly happens there, and moisture that gets in produces gas generation and accelerated ageing — a defect that passes every acceptance test and appears years later.

A transformer insulated and cooled by air or solid resin instead of oil. It carries no fire load and no oil-containment requirement, so it can sit inside a building, but it is larger, noisier and less efficient than an equivalent oil-filled unit and does not scale as far up in rating.

Debt service coverage ratio: the cash a project earns in a period divided by the debt payments due in it. Lenders size a loan so that the ratio stays above a floor in their downside case, which is why a merchant battery borrows less per megawatt than a tolled one.
Two classes of stock with different votes per share, so founders can keep control of the company while owning a minority of its economic value.
Equipment with two power supplies fed from two independent paths, so either path can be lost or worked on without the load noticing. It is what makes a whole side of a data hall maintainable at once.

Qualifying two suppliers for the same item so neither can hold the buyer hostage on price or availability. It costs money — two qualifications, two tool sets, split volume that raises unit cost — which is why it is an argued decision rather than a default.

The daily shape of demand left for conventional generators once solar output is subtracted — a deep midday trough and a steep evening climb, drawn as a duck's back and neck. It is the reason storage is valued for shifting energy a few hours rather than for days.
How long a storage plant can discharge at full power (energy divided by power, MWh ÷ MW). Duration decides which grid jobs a battery can do — most US grid-scale projects run a few hours.

A power room built and wired in a factory, tested as a unit, then shipped to site as a walk-in enclosure — switchgear, transformers, controls, lighting, HVAC and cable already in place. It converts skilled field electrical labour into factory labour and moves the schedule risk from the site to the shop, at the price of shipping weight, crane access and a design frozen much earlier.

A landowner's grant of a right to use a strip of land — for a transmission line, the right to build and maintain towers and conductors across a farm. A long line needs thousands; the ones a developer cannot buy voluntarily are the ones it seeks by eminent domain.

The Experimental Breeder Reactor II, a sodium-cooled fast reactor that ran at Idaho from 1964 to 1994 and in 1986 survived deliberate loss-of-flow and loss-of-heat-sink tests at full power with no operator action. Most US fast-reactor design heritage traces to it.

Running a static UPS with the load on the raw supply through the bypass and the conversion stage idling in reserve, lifting efficiency toward 98–99 percent. The bet is that the unit can detect a supply failure and transfer back to the inverter inside the servers' hold-up time, for every kind of fault — which is exactly what the mode's critics doubt.

The share of a company's profits and value an investor is entitled to, as distinct from control. CDPQ holds 52.4 per cent economic ownership of Invenergy Renewables while management remains the managing member that runs the business.

Effective load carrying capability: how much of a resource's nameplate a grid operator counts toward meeting peak — its accredited capacity. A four-hour battery or a solar farm is credited well below nameplate and a gas plant close to it, so accreditation decides how many megawatts of storage a utility must build to satisfy a reserve requirement and how much a battery earns in a capacity market.

A public utility commission whose members are chosen by voters rather than appointed by a governor. Its decisions on rates and plants carry directly into election campaigns, so affordability politics reach the docket faster than in an appointed state — and a single election can change who decides the next case.

Colorado's name for the integrated resource plan: a two-phase docket in which the commission first approves the need and the resource envelope, then a competitive solicitation is run and the commission selects the winning bids from the utility's shortlist in a second decision. Phase two is where the developers, and therefore the equipment, are actually chosen.

Electric service agreement: the contract between a utility and one large customer that fixes the megawatts to be served, the term, the minimum bill, collateral and exit terms — the document that turns a request for load into an obligation the utility can finance a plant against.

The step in cell manufacture where active material is mixed into a slurry, coated onto metal foil in a continuous web and dried, to a closely controlled thickness. Unevenness makes some of the electrode work harder than the rest, producing a cell that looks normal when new and ages unevenly.

How thickly the active material is coated onto a cell's current collectors. Thick electrodes hold more energy per litre and make the ions travel further; thin ones deliver current hard and store less. It is the single design choice that separates a power cell from an energy cell.

The industry of building electronics for other companies, spanning bare circuit-board assembly through full product assembly, test, distribution and repair. Its economics are volume and purchasing scale, so margins are thin and the winners are large.

A steel plate, anchor bolt, rail or bracket cast into concrete while it is wet, so something can later be bolted to it. Once the pour has cured, a missing embed becomes a drilled, tested and disputed repair.

The regulatory class for a stationary engine that runs only when the normal supply fails, plus a small annual allowance of hours for testing and maintenance. The class is what lets a backup fleet be permitted quickly and without the strictest emission controls — and it is lost the moment the same engines are run for prime power, peak shaving or a demand-response payment.

The area around a reactor within which off-site emergency plans must exist. Shrinking it is one of the concrete practical claims small designs make, and it is decided by the regulator against the source term, not by the vendor.

The legal power to take private land for a public use in exchange for compensation. A transmission line with a state certificate can use it against holdout landowners, which is why certificates are fought so hard in court.

Verified emission reductions bought elsewhere in the same airshed to compensate for a new source's emissions, required at better than one-to-one where the air already fails a standard. Where earlier reductions have been made and sold the market can be empty, and the constraint stops being financial and becomes absolute.

Energy management system: the supervisory software that decides when a storage plant charges and discharges — following price signals, grid instructions, or a contract — and coordinates the PCS and BMS to do it.

The voltage at which a discharge is declared over — chosen by the system rather than by the chemistry, because below it the inverter can no longer work with what the string is delivering. Set it lower and you buy minutes at the cost of life.

The point at which an asset stops being worth operating in its current duty — an economic judgment, not a technical failure. A storage system that has reached the bottom of its guaranteed capacity curve still holds most of its original energy, so whether it retires depends on what its site and connection can still earn.

The moment new electrical infrastructure is first put under live voltage and proven, with the utility present. It is the line between contracted megawatts and connected ones: before it, a connection agreement is a promise; after it, power can actually flow, and every schedule upstream of it is measured against this date.

Buying electricity when it is cheap (midday solar, overnight) to sell it when it is dear (evening peak). For a battery the profit is the price spread minus round-trip losses, and it is the revenue left once ancillary-service prices fall.

A battery optimized for how much it holds and how many times it can be emptied and refilled — sized by hours of duration and judged on cycle life and cost per stored unit. A grid storage container is the archetype, and it is the near-inverse of a power battery in almost every design choice.

The part of a bill priced per kilowatt-hour consumed — fuel and the variable cost of running plants. For a flat, always-on load it is large in total but it is the demand charge, not the energy charge, that decides whether the customer has paid for the capacity built to serve it.
An extra federal tax credit for projects sited in places with closed coal plants or mines or high fossil-fuel employment. Building a battery on a retired coal station earns it.

How much energy a cell stores per litre — or per kilogram — of itself. It is the figure of merit for a grid or vehicle cell, and it trades directly against the electrode design that lets a cell deliver current hard.

A grid connection that lets a project sell energy but carries no guarantee it can be counted toward the region's capacity requirement, and no right to be served firmly when the network is constrained. It is cheaper and faster to obtain than a full capacity connection, and the trade is made explicitly at the study stage.

A wholesale market design with no capacity market: generators are paid only for the energy they actually sell, and the incentive to build new plant comes from prices that spike when supply is scarce. ERCOT is the US example — no auction pays a plant to exist, so no commission certifies one, and whether a plant gets built is a private investment decision made against expected scarcity prices.

A site where large generation, storage and a large customer — a data centre, a hydrogen plant — are built together behind one grid connection, so most of the power never crosses the public grid. The developer sells the whole package rather than power alone.

Placing a large new electricity consumer — typically a data centre — at a site that already holds a grid connection built for generation or storage, so the consumer inherits the connection rather than joining the queue for a new one. The scarce asset being monetised is the interconnection position, not the equipment.

A contract in which a utility or public power agency pays a fixed fee for the right to use a battery's capacity for a term of years, leaving dispatch to the buyer. It is the public-power form of a tolling agreement.

The total quantity of energy a battery moves over its life, and the budget a long-dated capacity guarantee is really written against. Cycles, depth of discharge, rate and temperature all spend it, which is why an operating decision to cycle harder consumes warranty life the owner has already paid for.

The class of exposures created by deploying technologies faster than their loss history exists — batteries, hydrogen, floating wind, grid-scale power electronics. Underwriters price it with engineering judgment and standards compliance because the actuarial record they normally rely on has not been written yet.

The compressor, combustor and high-pressure turbine at the heart of a gas turbine — in an aeroderivative machine, the same core that powered an airliner. Because it is removed and replaced as a module, an overhaul is a swap measured in days rather than a rebuild measured in weeks, and whoever holds spare cores holds the plant's availability.

The licensed engineer who signs and seals a project's design and carries legal responsibility for it. On a turnkey EPC job it works for the contractor; on a multi-contract job the owner's engineer may hold the seal — which decides who answers when the design is wrong.

Raising the share of the fissile isotope uranium-235 above the 0.7% found in nature. The higher the enrichment, the more compact a core can be — and the tighter the security and transport rules become.

What a whole business is worth including its debt. Equity value is what the owners receive after the debt is counted, so a USD 7 billion enterprise value with USD 3 billion of equity value implies about USD 4 billion of debt.

The bundle of local approvals — zoning, annexation, site plan, permits, sometimes a development agreement — that lets a site be built as intended. Entitled land with power is what a utility-first developer sells.

The shorter form of federal environmental review under NEPA; when it ends in a finding of no significant impact (FONSI) no full environmental impact statement is needed, which can shorten a permit review by a year or more.

A contract in which a buyer purchases the renewable-energy certificates from a project without taking the electricity, which is sold into the grid. Meta's 2024 Invenergy deals were structured this way; the buyer gets the clean-energy claim, the project gets a fixed revenue stream.

A verified statement of a product's environmental impact across its life, prepared to a defined methodology so that two products can be compared on the same basis. It functions commercially like a certification: procurement rules and public tenders increasingly require one, so without it some buyers are simply unavailable.

The US emission stage most large standby data-center engines are certified to, available because an engine that only runs in emergencies is regulated far more loosely than one that runs for a living. It is why the same engine block is sold as a cheap Tier 2 standby set and an expensive Tier 4 prime set.
Engineering, procurement, and construction: the contractor model that delivers a plant turnkey under one contract — and the label for the firms that do it.

A thin crystal layer grown on top of a wafer to a precisely controlled thickness and doping. In a power device it is the drift region, so its quality sets both the voltage the part can hold off and how many good parts a wafer yields.

The engineered concrete base under a transformer, generator, chiller or tower, sized for its weight, its dynamic loads and its maintenance access. It has to exist before the equipment can be set, which puts it on the critical path.

An order to buy machinery — here generators — outright, with delivery on a schedule, as opposed to a power-purchase agreement in which someone else owns the plant and sells the output. The buyer owns the risk and the asset.

A short-dated revolving loan secured on equipment — turbines, transformers, switchgear — that funds progress payments until a permanent financing or a lease refinances it. Lenders to a pre-revenue developer write tenant tests into it: MUFG's line steps up amortisation if no 400 MW lease exists by a set date.

The share of a utility's regulatory capital structure funded by equity rather than debt. Regulators set it for ratemaking regardless of how the company actually finances itself. A higher equity ratio raises the allowed return in dollars, because equity earns the authorized return on equity while debt earns only its interest cost.
The investor capital a manager has raised and can deploy, measured before any borrowing. It sits below assets under management, which counts the borrowed money and the assets bought with it.

The Texas grid operator. An energy-only market with its own interconnection process — faster to connect, more volatile to operate in — which is why so much US storage and data-center buildout lands in Texas.

An employee stock ownership plan: a trust that holds company shares on behalf of employees, who receive an ownership account rather than buying in. It is a retirement plan and an ownership structure at once.

The European Union's emission stage for non-road and stationary engines — the counterpart to the US EPA tiers, and stricter than Tier 4 on particle number. A gen-set sold into both markets is certified twice, which is one reason European and American versions of the same product carry different after-treatment.

Enterprise value divided by earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation — the multiple buyers pay for a business's operating cash earnings; for operating renewable portfolios it prices the contracted cash flows.
The heat exchanger where the refrigerant boils and takes heat out of the water being chilled. In a chiller it is where the useful cooling actually happens.

One quintillion (10^18) hash attempts. Fleet sizes are quoted in exahashes per second (EH/s); a single modern mining machine contributes a few hundred terahashes per second, so an exahash is thousands of machines.

The chance that a loss of a given size or larger occurs in a year, usually drawn as a curve from small frequent losses to rare enormous ones. A '1-in-100-year loss' is a point on this curve, not a schedule — it means a 1% chance each year.

A policy that sits above the primary property policy and pays only once losses exceed the layer beneath it. Large plants build a tower of such layers because no single insurer will carry the whole replacement value.

The DC current fed to a synchronous machine's rotor winding to create its magnetic field. Raising it lifts the output voltage and the reactive power the machine supplies; the automatic voltage regulator adjusts it continuously, and it is how a rotary UPS or a synchronous condenser holds voltage through a disturbance.

What a large customer owes if it leaves a utility contract before the term ends — typically the remaining minimum bills, or the unrecovered cost of the plant and wires built for it. With the term, the ramp and the credit support it is one of the four terms that make a data-center tariff financeable.
The valve or orifice that drops the high-pressure liquid refrigerant back to evaporator pressure, cooling it as it goes. The cheapest component in the loop and the one that meters the whole machine.
A contractual right, not an obligation, for a customer to take more capacity later at pre-agreed terms. Headlines count options as if exercised; balance sheets do not.
Clay that swells when it takes on water and shrinks when it dries, moving whatever sits on it. It is treated by removing it, stabilising it, or spanning over it — never by ignoring it.

The share of premium consumed by acquisition costs — broker commission above all — plus administration. It is the half of the combined ratio a carrier controls by choosing its distribution, which is why a delegated-authority or direct model is an expense-ratio argument before it is anything else.

A multiplier applied to a contractor's workers' compensation premium, derived from its claim history against the expected history for its trade and size — above one is worse than average, below one better. Because it is computed from claims that have already closed, it prices the past by several years and cannot recognise a firm that has genuinely changed.

Government rules that restrict which products, technologies or data may be shipped to which countries or buyers without a licence; for AI, the rules that govern where advanced chips and servers may be sent and who may run them.

A formal move of the contractual completion date in response to a delay the contractor is not responsible for, stopping the daily damages clock. It grants time, not necessarily money — whether costs follow depends on whether the delaying event was merely excusable or also compensable.

The unincorporated land beyond a city's limits over which the city holds some planning control. Releasing a parcel from a city's ETJ moves it to the county, which in Texas cannot zone, impose moratoria or deny permits.
The European rules capping and reducing fluorinated-gas supply and banning specific uses on a schedule. It runs ahead of the US phasedown and is why some product lines change in Europe first.

The building's own cooling-water loop — the plant side of a coolant distribution unit — connected to chillers, cooling towers or dry coolers where the heat finally leaves the site. Larger, at whatever temperature the plant can make, and treated to plant rather than electronics standards, it never touches the servers.

A power-chain design that splits the two jobs a converter normally does — holding the voltage steady (regulation) and changing its level (transformation) — into separate stages, so each can be built where it works best. The regulator lives upstream where the current is small, and a fixed-ratio current multiplier lives next to the load where the current is enormous.

Testing assembled equipment at the manufacturer's works, with the customer present, before it ships. It catches wiring and logic errors while the fix is cheap and the gear is still accessible — but it can only prove what can be simulated in a shop, so an integrated test on site under real load is still the thing that proves the system.

Flexible AC transmission systems: the family of power-electronic devices — shunt and series compensation, STATCOMs, phase shifters — that make power flow in an AC network controllable instead of merely the arithmetic consequence of impedance.

Reinsurance bought one risk at a time, underwritten individually. A carrier uses it for a single account too large or too odd for its treaty — a first-of-its-kind battery plant, a hyperscale campus — and pays for the bespoke look.

The investment vehicle of a wealthy family, which can own operating businesses outright and hold them without a fund's fixed life. A family-owned developer answers to no limited partners and need not sell on a schedule.

Selling part of a project or portfolio — often a majority — to a long-term owner while keeping a stake and the operating role. It recycles a developer's capital into the next project; WEC Energy Group's majority ownership of Invenergy-built solar plants is the pattern.

An ERCOT ancillary service that pays a battery to inject power within a fraction of a second when grid frequency drops. Batteries are almost the only resource fast enough, which made it an early revenue source for Texas batteries.

A reactor that fissions with unmoderated, high-energy neutrons. Fission is less likely per neutron, so the fuel must be more enriched and the core more compact — but the neutrons that are left can do things thermal neutrons cannot.

The current that flows into a short circuit before a breaker clears it — many times the normal load current. A protection scheme needs enough of it to be sure the right breaker trips fast: a rotating machine delivers a large surge from its stored magnetic energy, while an inverter can supply only a little more than its rating, which changes how the downstream protection must be designed.

The portion of assets under management that actually pays a management fee. Total AUM includes money committed but not yet drawn, co-investment that pays nothing, and assets in wind-down — so fee-earning AUM is the number that drives revenue.

The profit an asset manager makes from management fees alone, before any share of investment gains. It is the recurring, predictable half of a manager's earnings, and analysts weight it more heavily than performance income because it does not depend on selling anything.

A support payment made on top of whatever the market pays, rather than instead of it. Because it adds to the price signal instead of replacing it, the generator still has a reason to produce when the system most wants the power — the main design advantage over a fixed feed-in tariff.

A fixed price per megawatt-hour paid to a generator for a set term, usually with an obligation on somebody to take the output. It removes almost all risk and therefore deploys capacity quickly, but it gives no reason to generate at valuable times — which is why markets that use one to start typically replace it with a premium or an auction.

Foreign entity of concern: a US legal designation (tied to China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea) that disqualifies projects and products with too much such involvement from federal tax credits — a central bankability question for China-linked battery supply.

The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission: the US regulator of interstate transmission, wholesale power markets and the regional grid operators. State commissions set retail rates and certify plants; FERC sets the transmission tariff and approves the market rules and interconnection procedures the state-level story sits on top of.

How most interstate transmission is priced: a formula, approved by FERC, that turns the transmission owner's booked costs and rate base into an annual revenue requirement, updated every year without a contested case. It is the reason transmission is a utility's most predictable earnings line and why a regional plan award converts into earnings so smoothly.

The 2023 order directing the North American reliability organisation to write mandatory standards for inverter-based resources — the instrument that turned ride-through from a voluntary engineering standard into an enforceable obligation on transmission-connected plants.

Funds from operations: the cash a company generates from running its business before working-capital swings. Rating agencies judge a utility mainly on FFO as a percentage of its debt, so a large capital plan financed with borrowing pushes that ratio down — and a utility whose ratio approaches the agency's stated downgrade threshold has to raise equity, sell an asset or slow the plan.

Interest a broker earns on premium it is holding in trust between collecting it from the client and paying it to the carrier. It is real income that rises and falls with short-term interest rates rather than with anything the broker did, so it flatters results when rates rise and reverses when they fall.

An on-site inspection and test of an installed or one-off product that was not factory-certified, ending in a serialised label from a recognised evaluation agency — the route by which a custom or low-volume energy-storage installation gets an accepted mark in Canada or the United States.

A single number that multiplies a device's on-resistance by a switching-related charge, so two switches can be compared on conduction and switching cost together. Lower is better, and it is how a datasheet argument about one material beating another is usually settled.
The point at which a project's owner formally commits the capital to build; before FID a project has permits and designs but no binding commitment to spend.

The date on which a project's loan agreements become effective and money can be drawn: every condition precedent satisfied, every adviser's report delivered. Construction schedules, equipment slots and tax-credit deadlines all hang on hitting it.
The fund or firm that owns a company's equity and can write the next cheque. Lenders price a project partly on who the sponsor is, and a change of sponsor can change the terms of every loan.

Dividing a building with rated walls and floors so that a fire and its smoke stay in one part of it for a stated number of hours. Every penetration through such a wall has to be sealed to the same rating.

How hot the gas is where it first meets the turbine blades — the single number a gas turbine's efficiency and output track most closely. Every extra hundred degrees buys efficiency and costs materials science: single-crystal blades, ceramic coatings and cooling air bled from the compressor, which is itself a loss. Modern heavy-duty machines are described by class as 1,600°C or 1,650°C.

The grid operator's last resort: ordering utilities to cut power to ordinary customers because supply cannot meet demand. Texas's 2025 large-load law ties the biggest customers to it — during an emergency the operator may direct a large load to run its backup generation or curtail before, or instead of, cutting homes.

A contract obliging a pipeline to move a stated quantity of gas every day. Its cheaper alternative, interruptible transportation, can be curtailed when the pipeline is constrained — typically in extreme weather, which is exactly when a plant depending on it can least afford to stop.

Adding a controllable resource — gas engines, turbines or a long-duration battery — to a renewable site so the customer's load is met in the hours the sun and wind cannot cover. It is what turns a solar-and-wind campus into round-the-clock supply.

A formal check of the first units off a production tool against every dimension and requirement on the drawing. Passing it is what turns a prototype process into an approved one, and it is a contractual milestone, not a courtesy.

The first unit of a new design, which pays for every lesson the design has not yet learned. Its cost is not evidence about the tenth unit, and treating it as such is the commonest error in reading a new-technology cost claim.

The fraction of units that pass every manufacturing step without rework. It is a quality measure and a cost measure at once — a plant can buy a low escape rate with heavy inspection and rework, which shows up here — so it is only informative alongside the rate of defects that actually escape.
The date a company closes its accounting year, which need not be 31 December. Comparing two companies' annual results without checking their year-ends can compare different twelve-month periods.

Splitting a heavy nucleus into lighter fragments, releasing energy and two or three free neutrons. Those neutrons are what make a chain reaction possible: the energy is a by-product of a neutron economy.

How fast a flame front travels through a fuel-air mixture. Hydrogen's is several times methane's, which is the root of most of the engineering in hydrogen-capable combustors: a flame that outruns the incoming mixture stops sitting where it was designed to sit.

A premixed flame travelling upstream into the burner it should be sitting in front of, because the mixture's flame speed has overtaken the flow feeding it. Hardware not designed for it melts. It is the specific failure mode that limits how much hydrogen a dry low-NOx combustor can take.

The point at which mining machines stop covering even their electricity cost, so running them destroys value and switching them off costs nothing. Difficulty only ever ratchets up and the halving only ever cuts revenue, so stranding is a scheduled outcome rather than a risk.

Continuous operating data gathered from every system a supplier has installed. It is what makes a long-dated performance guarantee priceable rather than guessed, surfaces failure patterns invisible at a single site, and feeds the next product design — which is why a large installed base is a technical asset and not only a sales record.

Connecting a very large load sooner in exchange for accepting curtailment when the network is constrained. It works because interconnection studies otherwise assume the load draws its full demand at the system's worst hour, so a load that can be told to stop needs far less reinforcement built for it.

Measurable — sometimes visible — fluctuation of voltage caused by a load that changes fast and repeatedly. It is the classic symptom of a large swinging load connected at a point that is not strong enough for it.

The amount an activity can slip before it becomes critical and starts moving the completion date. Its decisive property is that it is consumed by whoever uses it first, so a slow approval can spend the contractor's cushion for a problem it has not yet had — which is why contracts increasingly state explicitly who owns it.

The small continuous voltage held across a standby battery to keep it full without overcharging it. Nearly all of a UPS battery's life is spent floating, and the float voltage together with the room temperature decides how long that life is.

How level and how wavy a finished concrete floor is, expressed as F-numbers measured within days of the pour. A floor flat enough for an office is not necessarily flat enough for a row of racks on castors.

The weight per unit area a floor is allowed to carry. It decides where battery strings, large UPS frames and transformers may stand, and in retrofits it settles more equipment arguments than price does.

Making every rack on a shared coolant header receive its share of flow, since coolant takes the easiest path and the nearest or least-restricted racks would otherwise starve the far ones. Done with balancing valves or orifices at each manifold, reverse-return piping and a pump held to a pressure setpoint.

The practice of passing contractual obligations from a prime contract down through each subcontract tier. Where a required clause fails to flow down, the obligation usually stays with the prime contractor — which is how a prime becomes liable for a lower-tier subcontractor's wage violations.

Energy stored as rotation — half the moment of inertia times speed squared — in a heavy rotor or a fast light one on low-friction bearings, sometimes in a vacuum. It gives very high power for seconds, essentially unlimited cycles and no chemical aging, and its state of charge is simply its speed. In a UPS it covers a generator start; as a battery for hours it is the wrong tool.

Failure modes and effects analysis: a systematic enumeration of how each part of a design or process could fail, how likely and how detectable each mode is, and what is done about the ones that matter. Its value is the discipline of having thought about undetectable failures before they happen.
An additional investment by an existing shareholder in a later funding round of the same company, used to keep or increase its stake as the company grows.
How much protected power a machine delivers per square metre of floor it stands on. Where saleable white space is the scarce good, it is a commercial argument written as a specification.

A contract clause excusing performance made impossible by defined events outside either party's control. On a construction schedule its practical role is narrow: ordinary bad weather is priced into the programme as the contractor's risk, and only the genuinely abnormal reaches this clause.

The share of time a generating unit is unavailable because something broke, as opposed to planned maintenance. Capacity markets use it to discount what a plant is credited with: a unit that fails often is worth fewer accredited megawatts than its nameplate.

The gap between a predicted value — of price, generation or demand — and what actually happened. In storage optimisation it is usually the dominant source of lost revenue: an optimiser fed a poor forecast makes confident decisions that turn out wrong, and no amount of solver sophistication recovers it.

A non-US company listed in the United States that reports under a lighter regime than a domestic filer — annually on Form 20-F or 40-F rather than quarterly on 10-K and 10-Q, and often under international rather than US accounting rules.

The registration form an investment adviser files annually with the SEC; Part 1 discloses regulatory assets under management, employee count, client mix and fund vehicles, making it the audited-grade size record for a private fund manager.

The short notice a US company or fund files with the SEC after selling securities privately without registration; it discloses the amount sold, the number of investors and the placement agents — often the only public record of a private fund's size.

A rate mechanism that resets a utility's rates every year by formula — actual earned return compared with an allowed band, with automatic adjustment — instead of a full contested rate case every few years. It cuts regulatory lag for the utility and gives the commission a yearly look at earnings; Entergy's Louisiana, Arkansas and Mississippi companies run on one.

Selling a share of next year's expected output forward at a fixed price before the year begins, so the revenue is known rather than discovered. A fleet's hedge ratio is the fraction sold forward: a high ratio protects the budget and forfeits a price spike, a low one does the reverse.

An allowance built into a heat exchanger's rating for the film of scale, biology and dirt that will accumulate on its tubes. Real fouling beyond the allowance shows up as a widening approach and a rising kW/ton.

A factory that manufactures chips to other companies' designs and sells no chips of its own. A company that designs but does not manufacture is called fabless, and its roadmap is bounded by whatever manufacturing process and capacity its foundry will sell it.

Rejecting heat without running the compressors, by using a heat exchanger when the outdoor condition is cold enough to do the job directly. How many hours a year it works is a property of the climate and the water temperature chosen.

An engine architecture with no crankshaft, where the piston's travel is controlled electromagnetically rather than by mechanical linkage. Freeing the motion allows compression to be varied cycle by cycle, which is what lets such a machine change fuels in software and hold its efficiency at low load.

The fastest class of frequency-support service, responding automatically within seconds to arrest a change in grid frequency before it worsens. Known as FCR or primary control in Europe and as primary frequency response or fast frequency response in North America. Batteries are unusually well suited to it because they can change output almost instantly.

Equipment that turns power at one frequency into power at another — 50 Hz to 60 Hz between grids and ships, or grid power to the 400 Hz that aircraft systems use on the ground. Rotary versions do it with a motor-generator, static versions with a rectifier and an inverter.

A grid service in which a resource continuously adjusts its output up or down, second by second, following a signal from the system operator so that supply and demand stay matched and frequency stays near its target. Batteries are unusually good at it because they can reverse from charging to discharging almost instantly.

A resource that interconnects on the utility's side of the customer meter, like a small power plant, and is paid by wholesale markets or by contract — as opposed to behind-the-meter equipment on a customer's own site. Which side of the meter a project sits on decides the buyer, the contract, the rulebook, and the length of the sales cycle, which is why it is usually the first qualifying question asked.

A licensed, rated insurer that issues the policy paper for a risk it does not intend to keep, passing the risk on to a captive, an MGA's capacity providers or reinsurers for a fee. The buyer gets a policy from a rated carrier; the economics sit elsewhere.

Fixed Resource Requirement: PJM's alternative to bidding into the capacity auction, under which a utility commits to carry enough of its own accredited capacity to cover its load plus a reserve margin. It exempts that load from the auction's clearing price in both directions — no windfall when the price spikes, no relief when it collapses — and it is why two utilities in the same RTO can experience the same auction very differently.

The bill line that passes a utility's fuel and purchased-power costs straight through to customers, usually reset monthly or yearly with a true-up, and earning the utility no return. It is why gas prices show up on a bill within months while a new plant shows up only after a rate order.

Circulating stored diesel through filters and water separators so it stays usable. Standby fuel can sit for years, and diesel degrades — microbial growth, water ingress and asphaltene drop-out will clog filters at exactly the moment the set is finally asked to run.

A safety approach in which the barriers holding radioactivity are built into the fuel and reactor physics rather than a large pressure-tight building, so the plant can argue for a smaller structure and site footprint.

The fixed term — usually ten to twelve years — over which an investment fund must invest its money and return it to investors. A fund that owns a developer has to sell it or its projects before the fund closes, whatever the contracts' tenor.

Corrosion that starts when two different metals sit in one conductive fluid and form a battery, dissolving the less noble one. In a coolant loop the defence is matched wetted materials, plastic piping where metals would otherwise meet, and an inhibitor package kept at strength.

An electrical barrier — usually a transformer — that lets power cross from one circuit to another with no conducting path between them, so a fault on one side cannot reach people or equipment on the other. A non-isolated converter drops the barrier for simplicity and density where the chain already provides one upstream.
Gallium nitride: a wide-bandgap semiconductor suited to very fast, compact low-to-mid-voltage converters — one of the two key materials (with SiC) shrinking modern power electronics.

Switchgear whose live parts sit in a sealed enclosure filled with an insulating gas — historically sulphur hexafluoride, increasingly a lower-warming alternative — instead of open air. The gas holds off far more voltage per centimetre than air, so a gas-insulated substation occupies a small fraction of the footprint of an air-insulated one, which is why it is chosen where land is expensive or the site is indoors.

The pipe running from a gas main to a site, with the metering and pressure-regulating station at its end. It must be routed, permitted and built across land the buyer does not own, so it is an easement problem of the same kind as a power line — the fuel-side queue that on-site generation projects discover late.

The amount of charge that has to be pushed into a transistor's gate to turn it on. A device with less gate charge switches faster and costs the driver less power, which matters more the more times per second the circuit switches.

The deadline before a trading period after which bids into an electricity market can no longer be changed. It sets how far ahead a decision must be committed, and therefore how much of the decision rests on a forecast rather than on observation.

Generator set: an engine or turbine coupled to an alternator on one frame, with its controls, cooling and fuel system — the packaged unit a data center buys, rather than a bare engine. Rated in kilowatts or kilovolt-amperes at a declared duty: standby, prime or continuous.

A life insurer's own investment portfolio, funded by policyholder premiums, which must earn steady long-dated returns. Insurers put general-account money into infrastructure directly or through a captive fund, which is how a battery joint venture can be financed without a bank.

The firm that holds the construction contract with the owner and organises everyone who actually builds. Most general contractors subcontract every trade and add value through scheduling, coordination, procurement and risk-taking rather than through their own labour.
The firm that runs an investment fund, chooses its investments and earns a management fee and a share of profits. The limited partners supply the money; the general partner supplies the decisions.

A data-center development that builds its own power plant behind the fence — gas turbines, and in Fermi's case a reactor application — before it has a tenant, and treats the utility connection as a supplement rather than the source. The developer owns the delivery date and therefore the risk.

A breaker between the generator and its step-up transformer, rated for the very large currents a machine produces close up. It lets one unit be taken off and put back on the network without switching the whole high-voltage bay.

The transformer that lifts a generator's terminal voltage — usually tens of kilovolts — to transmission voltage. It is dedicated to one machine, sized to it, and its lead time is frequently the whole plant's.

The UK regulators' review of a reactor design independent of any site, run by the Office for Nuclear Regulation and the environment agencies; a design that passes can then be licensed for specific sites more quickly.

The programme of borings, samples and laboratory tests that establishes what is under a site before anything is designed for it. It is the cheapest work on a project and the source of its most expensive surprises.

A battery plant sized in gigawatt-hours of annual output rather than in units. Capacity is normally quoted as nameplate — the design figure — which can differ substantially from what a plant actually ships in its early years.

Grain-oriented electrical steel: the specialty magnetic steel every transformer core requires. Only a handful of mills worldwide produce it, and every announced transformer plant bids for the same tonnage — which is why transformer lead times, not capital, gate so many projects.

An accounting judgement about whether a company can meet its obligations for the next twelve months. When cash and committed facilities fall short, the filing must say the conditions 'raise substantial doubt' and then state management's plans; if the plans are judged sufficient, the doubt is 'alleviated' but the sentence stays in the filing.
The part of a purchase price above the value of the identifiable assets — paid for the team, the relationships and the expected future business rather than for anything on a balance sheet.

The US legal rule that the law cannot be copyrighted. In 2024 the Fifth Circuit applied it to hold that Canadian codes incorporated by reference into Canadian law could be reprinted in the United States without CSA's permission, even though Canadian courts had enforced CSA's copyright.

A relatively small fund raised by a developer or fund manager to supply its own share — often 5–10% — of the equity in the joint ventures it forms with institutional partners. Its 'buying power' is the total project value that share can control.

Graphics processing unit — a processor with thousands of simple cores designed to do the same operation on very many numbers at once. That shape turned out to suit neural networks far better than a conventional CPU, which is why the graphics part of the name is now mostly historical.

A large number of accelerators wired together with a high-speed network so they can work on one job. What makes it a cluster rather than a pile of servers is the interconnect and the software that keeps thousands of chips in step.
Government funding recognised in a company's income statement as work under a cooperative agreement is performed; for a pre-revenue reactor developer it can be the largest line above the loss.

A tradeable certificate created by a quota: suppliers must surrender a set number each year, and that obligation is what gives the certificate a price. Unlike a plain renewable energy certificate, which records an attribute of generation, this is a support instrument — and because both the certificate price and the power price float, projects relying on one are the hardest of the support schemes to finance.

A loan labelled under the Loan Market Association's Green Loan Principles because its proceeds fund eligible green assets such as batteries; a 'green structuring agent' certifies the use of proceeds. It widens the lender pool without changing the credit terms.

A utility rate schedule that lets a large customer buy the output and environmental attributes of a specific renewable project through the utility, so the customer gets green power without contracting directly with the developer.
A commitment by a grid operator to hold a stated amount of connection capacity for a customer at a named substation. It is the scarce asset behind a power-first site: without it the site is land.

The network operator's rulebook for how a connected plant must behave electrically — voltage and frequency response, reactive capability, ride-through and protection. Compliance is a separate programme from product safety certification, often witnessed on the energised plant, and is a common cause of late energisation delay.

An inverter that locks onto the grid's existing voltage wave and injects current into it — a surfer riding a wave someone else is making. It is the conventional mode and works well, but it cannot operate at all without a live grid to follow, so it contributes nothing during the outage it is standing beside.
An inverter that sets its own voltage and frequency like a traditional generator, rather than following the grid's. It lets storage stabilize weak grids and restart dead ones (black start).

A UPS whose battery is also allowed to work for the building or the grid — shaving a peak, answering a demand-response call, holding frequency — rather than sitting at float. It turns a stranded asset into an earning one and puts the backup duty into competition with the earning duty.

The total electrical capacity a data center draws or is built for, including cooling, power losses and support systems as well as the computers. A 168 MW critical-IT hall may need 240 MW gross; the utility sees the gross number.

What a retail electricity supplier collects from customers minus what the electricity and its delivery cost to procure. It is the number a retail business is actually run on, and it widens when wholesale prices fall faster than retail prices do.

The schedule of minimum energy a storage system must still hold at each year of its life. It is a floor rather than a forecast — the supplier's own expected curve sits above it — and it is steep early and flatter later, because capacity fade is fastest when cells are new.
A ceiling on cost that the builder commits to, above which it absorbs the overrun. What is inside the ceiling, what the contingency covers and who keeps the savings are the terms that matter.
Global warming potential: how much a kilogram of a gas warms the atmosphere over a period, relative to a kilogram of carbon dioxide. It is the number regulators use to rank refrigerants.

Tilting a solar tracker to a steep angle ahead of a forecast hailstorm so that stones strike the glass obliquely and lose most of their energy. Its benefit depends on the stow angle, how fast the tracker moves and the stone size; underwriters reward documented stow capability with lower rates or deductibles.

High-assay low-enriched uranium: fuel enriched above the roughly 5% of conventional reactors but below the 20% that counts as highly enriched. Compact fast cores need it, and almost nobody makes it yet.

Two switches in series across a supply with the load taken from the point between them. Almost every power converter is built from one or more of these, and most of what can go wrong in one is about what happens at the instant the pair change over.

A scheduled event, roughly every four years, that cuts the new bitcoin paid to miners per block in half. It is a step change in industry revenue with no offsetting change in cost, so it forces the least efficient capacity out.

Conditions in which insurers have less appetite than the market wants: prices rise, deductibles rise, limits shrink and terms narrow. Buyers feel it as a scramble for capacity; brokers earn more because commission is a percentage of a bigger premium.

Software designed to work across equipment from many manufacturers rather than only the vendor's own. In energy it is a purchasing criterion rather than a marketing phrase: a fleet assembled over a decade contains several brands, and software tied to one of them cannot see the rest.

Testing a real controller against a real-time simulation of the plant and grid it will run, so it cannot tell the difference. It is how faults during islanding, loss of the largest generator, or a violent load step with the battery nearly empty get exercised thousands of times — cases that could never be staged on a live site.

Distortion added to a clean AC waveform by loads that draw current in gulps rather than smoothly — rectifiers, drives, server power supplies. Harmonics overheat transformers and neutral conductors, nuisance-trip breakers, and distort the voltage other equipment sees; total harmonic distortion (THD) is the score, and under 5% is the common target.
The later years of a closed-end fund's life, after the investment period ends, when the manager stops buying and sells assets to return capital to investors.

Mining revenue per unit of computing power per day — typically dollars per petahash per second per day. It bundles the bitcoin price, network difficulty and transaction fees into one number, and it is the single figure that decides whether a machine earns more than the electricity it burns.

How many hash guesses a machine, a fleet or the whole network makes per second. Measured in terahashes (TH/s, a trillion per second) and exahashes (EH/s, a million million million per second). A miner's share of total network hashrate is roughly its share of the rewards.

High-bandwidth memory — memory chips stacked vertically and placed in the same package as the processor, connected by a very wide link. Its capacity and speed usually decide how large a model an accelerator can hold and how fast it can be fed, so it is often the binding constraint rather than the arithmetic.
A microreactor design that moves heat out of the core through sealed tubes in which a fluid evaporates at the hot end and condenses at the cold end, with no pumps and no coolant loop at all.

The efficiency yardstick for a thermal power plant: fuel energy in per unit of electricity out, so a lower number is better. It decides which plants a market dispatches first, hour by hour, and it is the same quantity as percentage efficiency quoted the other way up.

A chiller run so that the heat it rejects is sold or used rather than thrown away — hot water for a building or a district. Physically it is a heat pump; commercially it is a chiller with a second product.

Piping a data center's waste heat to a nearby user — a district heating network, a swimming pool, a fish farm — instead of rejecting it to the air. Cheap where the site is cold and the heat has a buyer; a planning-permission argument in Europe.

A large, stationary gas turbine designed from scratch for power generation rather than adapted from a jet engine: single-shaft, heavy castings, tens to hundreds of megawatts, built for long runs between overhauls rather than for light weight or fast starts. Manufacturers grade them by class — F, G, H, J — which is shorthand for firing temperature, and each class step buys efficiency.

A financial contract that fixes part of a project's future price without a physical buyer — the project sells power to the market and settles the difference with a bank or trader. It is how merchant solar and batteries create a bankable revenue line.

Higher heating value: a fuel's energy content counted with the water in the exhaust condensed back to liquid, so the heat of condensation is included. For natural gas it is about a tenth larger than the lower value, which means the same machine looks roughly ten percent less efficient when quoted on this basis.

High-performance computing — the classical supercomputing workload of physical simulation: weather, fluid dynamics, structural and nuclear modelling. It differs from AI work in needing high-precision arithmetic rather than tolerating low precision, which is why national laboratories still buy on double-precision performance.

The transmission tier — roughly 100 kV and up in the United States, with 230 kV, 500 kV and 765 kV the workhorse classes — used to move bulk power between regions and into a cluster of substations. Higher voltage carries more power over the same right-of-way with less loss, which is why the lines proposed for data-center corridors keep going up a class.

Hypothetical liquidation at book value: the accounting method that splits a tax-equity partnership's profit or loss by asking what each partner would receive if the project were liquidated at book value today. It is why a renewables owner's reported net loss can be far larger than its economic loss — most of it is allocated to the tax-equity investor.

How long a private-equity or infrastructure fund expects to own an asset before selling it, typically four to seven years for buyout capital and longer for infrastructure. The clock shapes when a sponsor starts preparing a sale or listing.

How long a server power supply can carry its load on internal capacitors after its input disappears — roughly 10 to 20 milliseconds. It is the physics referee for every power transfer: a switchover completed inside that window is invisible to the IT load, and one that misses it is an outage.

A parent corporation that owns several regulated operating utilities, each with its own territory, commission and rate base. Investors buy the parent; regulators regulate the subsidiaries — so one earnings call can describe five different regulatory relationships at once.

A developer whose product is the finished site — grading, roads, water, sewer, substation, zoning and permits — sold or leased to the vertical developer who builds the data center. Tract is the corpus's purest example; the buildings are somebody else's.

The division of a campus into site work and paper (horizontal: civil works, utilities, entitlements) and the building and everything inside it (vertical). A land developer that grows a vertical arm is choosing to capture the widest rung of the value ladder — powered to leased — rather than sell the parcel once.

Starting a turbine that is still warm from a recent shutdown, which is far quicker than starting one that has cooled — thick steam-turbine casings must be reheated slowly or they distort. Plants are quoted as hot, warm and cold start times, and the gap between them is why a machine that is cheap to run flat out can be expensive to use as a follower.

Removing or inserting a unit — a power supply, a converter shelf, a drive — while the rest of the system stays live. It works only because the unit and its slot were engineered for it: the connector sequence, the inrush control and the isolation of a failed unit are all deliberate design work.

Matching a site's electricity consumption to carbon-free generation in every hour, rather than netting annual totals. It is far harder than an annual match because it requires generation or storage available at 3am as well as at noon, which is why it is sold as a premium product.

Heat-recovery steam generator: the boiler that sits in a gas turbine's exhaust and makes steam from heat that a simple-cycle plant throws away. It is where a combined-cycle plant's extra third of output comes from, and it is also most of the extra equipment, the extra water treatment and the extra construction time.

High-temperature gas-cooled reactor: a reactor cooled by helium gas and moderated by graphite that runs far hotter than a water-cooled reactor (around 750°C outlet), so it can supply industrial steam as well as electricity.

High-voltage direct current: moving power as DC instead of AC — over long transmission links, and now inside the data center as the 800 VDC rack architecture. Fewer conversion stages and far less copper, at the cost of protection that cannot wait for an AC waveform to cross zero and extinguish the arc for it.

Hydrotreated vegetable oil: a renewable diesel made by hydrogen-treating fats and oils, chemically close enough to fossil diesel that many engines burn it with no hardware change.
