It is the lowest-friction way a standby fleet cuts lifecycle carbon, because the change is in the tank rather than the machine.

A fuel containing no carbon, so burning it produces no carbon dioxide. Its flame is very fast and hot, which brings the risk of the flame travelling back up the burner and raises nitrogen-oxide formation — so blending a modest fraction into an existing machine is a tuning exercise, while burning it neat is a combustion-system redesign.

Burning a hydrogen-natural-gas blend in a machine designed for gas. The percentage quoted is almost always by volume, and hydrogen carries about a third of methane's energy per unit volume — so a 30 percent by volume blend is only about ten to eleven percent of the energy and cuts carbon dioxide by roughly the same tenth. Reading a volumetric figure as an energy figure overstates the decarbonisation about threefold.

A side reaction at a battery's negative electrode in which water is split into hydrogen instead of the intended reaction occurring. It consumes charging current without storing energy, and in iron electrodes it is the main reason round-trip efficiency is low.
One of the giant cloud and platform operators that build and lease data-center capacity at gigawatt scale. Their capital spending sets the pace of the AI data-center buildout.

The heat made by current flowing through resistance: power lost equals current squared times resistance. Doubling the current through the same conductor quadruples the loss, which is why every power chain climbs to a higher voltage — and a lower current — for the long stretch and converts down only at the end.

Inverter-based resource: anything that reaches the grid through power electronics rather than through a spinning machine — solar, wind, and battery storage. The category exists because inverters behave differently from generators during a disturbance, so the reliability rules written for them are separate rules.

Installed capacity — the capacity-market construct used in New York, in which load-serving entities must buy enough capability to cover their peak demand plus a reserve. A storage project earns from it by being available when called, separately from any energy it sells.

Infection control risk assessment: the formal procedure for building inside or beside an operating healthcare facility — barriers, negative pressure, filtration, traffic routes. The discipline transfers directly to building beside a live data hall.

An international standard for communication between devices in electrical substations and power plants, widely used so that equipment from different suppliers can be monitored and controlled together. Speaking it at a plant's boundary is one of the ways an owner keeps the option of changing who operates the plant.

The international standard that classifies a UPS by how much of the supply's misbehavior reaches the load: VFD (voltage and frequency dependent — the supply passes through until it fails), VI (voltage independent — line-interactive, voltage corrected), and VFI (voltage and frequency independent — the load is fully isolated, as in double conversion or a rotary machine). Codes such as VFI-SS-111 add the output-waveform and transient grades so two makers' promises can be compared.

The international standard family for industrial control-system cyber security. A certification level against it states what a device's own defences were audited to — not that the network around it is safe.
The international safety standard for industrial lithium cells and batteries, stationary storage included. A certificate against it is the common passport for selling cells into other markets.

The international standard series for electrical energy storage systems — unit parameters, test methods, planning, safety and environmental requirements — that independent engineers and recommended practices cite when specifying how a grid battery is to be tested and accepted.

The American interconnection standard for distributed energy resources connecting to a distribution system. The 2018 edition replaced the older must-trip posture with graded ride-through obligations, and sorts resources into Categories A and B for reactive capability and Categories I, II and III for how far and how long they must ride through a disturbance.

The standard method for calculating arc-flash incident energy: given the available fault current, the gap between conductors, the enclosure and — critically — how long the protective device takes to clear, it returns the energy a worker at a stated distance would receive. Clearing time is the term the engineer can actually change, which is why arc-flash mitigation is usually a protection-settings problem.

The 2022 interconnection standard for inverter-based resources connecting to a transmission system — the large-plant counterpart to IEEE 1547. Voluntary as an IEEE document; it acquires force in the United States through the reliability standards that adopt its ride-through requirements.

The standard that sets harmonic-distortion limits at the point of common coupling — the property line where a facility's electrical system meets the utility. It draws the boundary so one customer's distorted loads cannot degrade a neighbor's power quality, and compliance is measured at that point rather than assumed.

The accounting rulebook used in most of the world outside the United States. It differs from US rules most visibly in letting companies carry some assets at current market value rather than at original cost.

Insulated-gate bipolar transistor: the silicon switch that static UPS inverters, drives and grid inverters have been built on for three decades — fast enough to chop DC into a clean sine wave thousands of times a second and rugged enough for megawatts. Silicon carbide is displacing it where the last points of efficiency matter.

A penalty paid when a market participant delivers more or less energy than it committed to deliver. It is the mechanism that makes a bid a promise rather than an intention, and it is why forecast quality has a direct cash consequence.

Running a battery's bidding and dispatch with the owner's own traders and software rather than handing it to a third-party optimiser or toller. The owner keeps the margin and carries the risk of being wrong about prices.

A coolant distribution unit built into the server rack itself — a few rack units of pumps, exchanger and filters serving that one cabinet. Its fault domain is one rack and it can be filled and tested off-site, at the cost of rack space, a pump per rack and a capacity ceiling.

A cabinet-sized coolant distribution unit standing in the row and feeding a shared header to several racks — the megawatt-class units the current AI rack generation is designed around. One unit and one facility connection serve up to a dozen racks, so the fault domain is the row unless a partner unit shares the header.

The thermal energy an arcing fault would deliver to a worker standing at a stated working distance, expressed in calories per square centimetre. It sets the protective clothing required to open the door, and it falls with anything that shortens the arc's duration — faster relay settings, a maintenance-mode switch, or an upstream device that sees the fault sooner.

A law or regulation adopting a privately written standard by citing it rather than reprinting it, so the standard's text becomes a legal requirement. It is how the Canadian Electrical Code, NFPA 855 and UL standards acquire legal force — and why their copyright is contested.

The technical diligence firm lenders hire to review a project on their behalf — the design, the equipment, the contracts, the production estimate. Its report is the gate to financial close, which makes the independent engineer, not the buyer, the audience a supplier's certifications and track record ultimately have to satisfy.

A company that owns power plants and sells their output but is not a regulated utility with captive customers. Its revenue comes from contracts and markets, so its cost of capital and its exposure to prices are both higher than a utility's.

The stabilizing effect of heavy spinning generator masses, which resist sudden changes in grid frequency and buy operators seconds to react. As synchronous plants retire in favor of inverter-connected wind, solar, and storage, that inertia has to be replaced — by synchronous condensers, or by grid-forming inverters imitating it electronically.

Running a finished model to produce an answer, as opposed to building it. Each request is small compared with training but there are enormous numbers of them, so inference rewards memory capacity, low latency and cost per answer rather than raw peak arithmetic.

A pooled investment vehicle that buys long-lived, cash-generating physical assets — pipelines, ports, transmission, power plants — on behalf of pension funds and insurers. It prices contracted cash flows, so a contracted battery fleet is a natural fit and a merchant one is not.

A rated measure of how well an enclosure keeps out solid objects and water, written as two digits — the first for dust, the second for water. Equipment and the assemblies inside it usually carry different ratings, because one is protecting against external weather and the other against events inside the box.

Chilling or humidifying the air entering a gas turbine's compressor to claw back the output that hot weather takes away. A turbine is a volumetric machine — it swallows a fixed volume per revolution — so hotter, thinner air means less mass, less fuel burned and less power, typically a fraction of a percent of output per degree Celsius.

Total harmonic distortion of the current a converter draws from its supply, as a percentage. A low figure means the machine looks like a plain resistor to the generator and the transformer upstream; a high one means that upstream plant has to be oversized to feed it.

The brief surge of current a device draws at the instant it is connected, as its empty capacitors charge in a rush. Uncontrolled, it can sag a shared bus, trip protection or pit a connector; precharge circuits exist to tame it.

The amount of limit insurers are collectively willing to put on a risk or a class of risk. For a managing general agent, capacity is the limit its carriers allow it to bind per location; when capacity is scarce the market is 'hard' and prices rise, when abundant it is 'soft'.

The asset class covering catastrophe bonds, collateralised reinsurance and sidecars — insurance risk packaged so pension funds and hedge funds can hold it. It is the alternative capital that now competes with traditional reinsurers on price.

An insurance policy that takes on defined performance or warranty risk from a supplier, so a buyer's exposure becomes the insurer's credit rather than the supplier's. It is expensive and heavily conditioned, and its exclusions often mirror the risks the buyer was most concerned about.

The commissioning stage in which the finished plant is failed on purpose under artificial load — utility dropped, engines started, transfers made, cooling recovered — to prove the pieces behave as one system rather than as a set of correct machines.

The signed contract between a project and the grid operator or utility that fixes the connection point, the capacity allowed, the upgrades the project must pay for and the date it must be ready. Signing it ends the study phase and is one of the rungs a buyer pays most for.
The waiting line for grid-connection studies and approval. Multi-year queues are one of the main bottlenecks for new data centers and storage plants.

The contract between a generator, its transmission owner and the grid operator setting out how the plant connects, what it may inject, and what equipment and studies the connection depends on. Changing what sits behind that connection generally means amending the agreement, which is a regulated filing rather than a private decision.
The temporary arrangements — alarms, exits, fire watch, access routes — that keep an occupied building safe while construction has disabled part of its permanent systems.

The voltage a rack or a server distributes between its main supply and the point-of-load converters — 12 volts in the older chain, 48 volts (often run at 54) in the modern one. Choosing it is a trade between the current the bus must carry, the safety rules it falls under, and how hard the final conversion becomes.

A second coolant circuit placed between the radioactive primary coolant and the water/steam side, so that a leak between sodium and water cannot happen inside the reactor. It costs efficiency and buys separation.

A tariff under which a large customer accepts that the utility may curtail its supply on short notice a set number of hours a year, in exchange for a lower rate. It lets the utility count on shedding that load at the system peak, which reduces the capacity it must build to serve everyone else.

A party admitted to a regulatory proceeding to represent an interest other than the utility's: consumer advocates, large industrial customers, environmental groups, municipalities, the commission's own staff. Intervenors file testimony proposing adjustments to the utility's request, and the gap between the filed request and the intervenors' recommendations frames what the commission ultimately decides.

A transaction between two entities under the same manager — a land fund selling a parcel to its sister campus fund. Valid and common, but it sets no market price: the buyer and the seller share an owner, and the price may be repaid to the sponsor from the buyer's own financing.

A converter that turns direct current into alternating current — the mirror image of a rectifier. It appears wherever DC has to be handed back to an AC world: on the output of a battery or solar array, inside a UPS, and between an electric vehicle's pack and its motor. A bidirectional one that does both jobs is a power conversion system.

A credit rating (BBB-/Baa3 or better) signalling low default risk. Debt rated investment grade can be sold to insurers and pension funds at lower interest; a project loan achieving it on the strength of an anchor contract is borrowing on the anchor's credit.

Earning revenue by letting other companies use patented technology under a royalty or fee instead of, or as well as, selling products. For a hardware company it turns a patent portfolio into a second business — and a lawsuit into a negotiation.

Integrated project delivery: a multi-party contract in which owner, designer and builder share a single risk-and-reward pool. It aligns incentives and requires an owner willing to work inside the team.

Integrated part-load value: a single efficiency number that weights performance at 100, 75, 50 and 25 percent load, because a chiller almost never runs at its design point. It uses standard-rating conditions.
Initial public offering: the first sale of a company's shares to the public on a stock exchange, priced by underwriters and followed by a lock-up period during which insiders may not sell.

Integrated resource plan: a regulated utility's commission-filed roadmap of what it expects to need and how it intends to procure it. Certified IRP megawatts are the real demand pipeline for an equipment supplier — they become purchase orders on a multi-year fuse.

Internal rate of return: the annual return that makes a project's future cash flows worth exactly what it costs today. Developers quote it to buyers; a falling battery price raises it because the same revenue is earned on less capital.

Running electrically disconnected from the grid, with on-site generation alone matching the load every second. There is no larger system to lean on, so frequency and voltage become the site's own problem — and so does restarting after a total loss.

A campus power system that generates, stores and balances its own electricity with no grid connection, or with the grid held in reserve. It trades a utility queue for the burden of running a power plant.

The international standard that defines how reciprocating gen-sets are rated, so a kilowatt from one maker means the same as a kilowatt from another. Its rating classes — emergency standby, limited-time, prime and continuous — differ in the hours a year the set may run and the average load it may carry, not in the hardware.

The independent system operator for the six New England states, which runs the region's wholesale energy, reserve and capacity markets. Its load centres are transmission-constrained, so where a resource sits inside the system matters as much as how big it is.

A gas turbine's output and efficiency quoted at internationally agreed reference conditions — 15°C, sea level, 60 percent relative humidity, no inlet or exhaust pressure loss. Real sites are hotter, higher, and always have ducting, so the site rating is always below the catalogue number and the gap is the first correction any honest plant calculation makes.

A governor mode that holds engine speed — and therefore frequency — at exactly its setpoint regardless of load, as opposed to droop, which lets speed fall slightly as load rises. An islanded plant needs one machine or one control loop holding frequency isochronously; paralleled machines otherwise fight each other for the load.

A UPS topology in which many units are joined in a ring through chokes: in normal operation each unit feeds its own load, and when one fails its load is picked up by all the others sharing through the ring rather than by one dedicated spare. It reaches N+1 with one spare across a very large block instead of doubling the plant, and it is the shape in which rotary UPS is sold at tens of megawatts.
The US investment tax credit: a percentage of a storage or solar project's cost returned as a federal tax credit. A core driver of BESS project economics, with bonus tiers for domestic content.

SPP's Integrated Transmission Plan: the yearly planning process in which the grid operator identifies the lines the plains grid needs, approves a portfolio and assigns projects to transmission owners, with cost allocation across the region. Its 2024 and 2025 portfolios were the largest in the operator's history and included the first 765 kV lines in its footprint.

In merger law, the position in which two or more shareholders can each block strategic decisions — budgets, sales, new campuses — regardless of share percentages. A company can be majority founder-owned and jointly controlled at once; the European Commission's clearance of Prime records exactly that.
Joint design manufacture — an arrangement in which buyer and manufacturer develop the product together, splitting the design work and, usually, arguing later about who owns which part of it.

A company formed by two parties that each contribute something — here an operator's projects and know-how and an investor's capital — and share the ownership. The economic split can differ from the headcount of members, so the unit terms matter more than the name.

The efficiency rating of a mining machine: how much energy it spends per trillion hash attempts. Lower is better. Because every miner sells the same product at the same price, this number and the price of electricity are almost the whole of a miner's competitive position.

The policy of retiring coal plants on a schedule while funding the workers and communities that depended on them. Colorado wrote it into law in 2019 with a 2030 carbon target and a state office; it is why the state's resource plans pair a coal retirement date with a replacement build and a community package in the same decision.

The shorthand for a provision in Texas's 2025 large-load law: the grid operator can require a very large customer to install equipment that lets the operator curtail it remotely during a firm load-shed emergency. In practice it is a curtailment protocol with the operator, not the customer, holding the switch.

The unit data-center rent is quoted in: dollars per kilowatt of reserved power per month. Always ask whether the kilowatts are critical IT load or total facility power (which includes cooling and losses) — the same dollar figure means very different rents on the two bases.
Electrical power drawn per ton of cooling delivered — the chiller industry's efficiency measure, where lower is better. It is the inverse of COP in different units.

Formal recognition by an authority that a laboratory or certification body is competent to test or certify against named standards — the layer above certification. In Canada the Standards Council of Canada accredits; in the United States OSHA recognises testing laboratories and ANSI accredits certifiers.

Sites a developer has bought or optioned ahead of any tenant, usually where utility capacity can be secured. Cheap to hold relative to the megawatts it can carry, and the raw material of every pipeline figure.

The rungs a data-center parcel climbs — raw land, entitled and serviced, powered (a dated utility instrument), leased — and the idea that price and risk move with the rung, not the acreage. Only the leased rung supports large debt; the powered rung is the widest, slowest and least in the developer's control.

A single customer — a data centre, an industrial plant — big enough that the grid must plan for it individually. Texas SB 6 draws the line at 75 MW; loads above it face curtailment rules, security deposits and co-location review.

The utility's filed contract with a very large customer, approved by the state commission, that fixes the customer's minimum take, deposits, term and share of grid upgrades. It is the regulator's instrument for allocating the cost of serving a gigawatt-scale campus.

The process by which a very large new customer — a data center, a hydrogen plant, a crypto mine — is studied and connected to the transmission system. In ERCOT the wires utility runs the studies and builds the substation, the grid operator reviews the request against the wider system, and since 2025 the state's rules set fees, security and curtailment terms for it. It is a load process, distinct from the generator interconnection queue.

A utility rate class written specifically for very large customers such as data centers: long contract terms, minimum-take obligations, exit fees, and collateral. It is the filter that separates real demand from speculative interconnection requests, and the instrument that turns AI load into something a utility can plan and finance against.

A transformer at transmission scale — hundreds of megavolt-amperes, custom-designed, built to order, shipped in pieces and assembled on site. Lead times run to years, and the binding constraint is test bays and skilled winders rather than steel.

A full-scale burn of a complete battery enclosure with suppression switched off, set beside neighbouring units at installation spacing, to observe whether fire propagates and what heat the neighbours receive. Distinct from UL 9540A's cell-to-installation propagation test; mandatory under NFPA 855's 2026 edition and specified by CSA C800.

The energy a substance absorbs or releases while changing phase, at constant temperature. It is far larger than the energy involved in warming the same mass by a few degrees, which is why refrigeration boils a fluid rather than merely warming one.

Feeding a processor from converters mounted on the board beside the package, with the current running sideways through the board's copper for the last centimetre. It is the conventional arrangement, and the one that runs out of room and out of copper as chip currents climb.

Levelised cost of energy: the lifetime cost of a plant divided by the lifetime energy it produces, discounted. It compresses capital cost, fuel, operating cost, capacity factor and the cost of money into one number, and hides all five.

A lead-acid battery with carbon added to the negative plate. The carbon slows the sulphation that kills ordinary lead cells in partial-state-of-charge duty and lets them accept charge faster — which is why the chemistry survived in telecom and off-grid work rather than dying with the rest.

The layered sensing that finds coolant where it should not be: conductive trace loops around each cold plate reporting through the server's management controller, sensing cable along manifolds and drip trays, and level sensors on the CDU reservoir. Detection triggers isolation of the branch and a clean shutdown before water reaches live boards.

A gas-engine combustion strategy that burns with excess air, which lowers peak flame temperature and so forms far less nitrogen oxide inside the cylinder. It is how a natural-gas gen-set meets a tight air permit with little after-treatment, at the cost of a slower response to sudden load steps than a diesel.

The empirical observation that unit cost falls by a roughly constant percentage each time cumulative output doubles. It is the whole economic argument for making reactors in a factory in series rather than on a site once.
A bacterium that grows in warm stagnant water and can be dispersed in aerosols, which is why open cooling towers carry a mandated water-treatment and testing regime.

Bank guarantees a developer posts instead of cash — to a grid operator for interconnection deposits, to a customer as contract security, to a supplier. A large LC facility is a sign of a large pipeline, because every queue position and contract needs one.

A signed statement that two parties intend to do a deal on outlined terms, usually non-binding. It reserves capacity and starts diligence; it is not a contract, and either side can walk away — as anchor tenants do.
Low-enriched uranium: uranium enriched to less than 5% U-235, the fuel of the existing light-water fleet and the widely available enrichment product.

Lithium iron phosphate: a lithium-ion battery chemistry using an iron-phosphate cathode. It trades some energy density for lower cost, longer cycle life, and much better thermal stability than nickel-based chemistries — which is why it dominates grid-scale storage.

Lower heating value: a fuel's energy content counted with the water in the exhaust left as vapour, which is what a normal plant actually does with it. Efficiency and heat-rate figures are usually quoted on this basis, and comparing one against a higher-value figure is the most common error in the field.

An instruction to start a bounded slice of work — usually engineering, long-lead ordering and mobilisation — at an agreed price, months before full notice to proceed is possible. It exists because equipment lead times are longer than the financing process, and when it funds equipment directly it also removes the largest cash exposure from the contractor's balance sheet.

An investor in a fund — a pension plan, an insurer, a sovereign fund — that puts up the money but takes no part in running it. CDPQ is both a limited partner in many funds and, at Invenergy, a direct owner.

A loan to a project entity secured on that project's assets and lease, with little or no claim on the sponsor's other assets if it fails. The standard form of data-center construction debt, sized to the signed lease rather than to the developer's balance sheet.

The older HVDC converter type, built from thyristors that need the AC network's own voltage to turn them off. Rugged and efficient at very high power, but it cannot energise a dead network and it consumes reactive power while working.

A UPS that normally passes the supply through while a transformer or inverter trims the voltage, stepping in fully only when the supply fails. Cheaper and more efficient than double conversion, at the cost of a short break the load must be able to ride.

A generating machine in which a piston drives magnets past coils in a straight line, inducing current directly instead of turning a shaft. Compressing a very lean mixture until it reacts all at once, with no flame front, keeps temperatures low enough that little nitrogen oxide forms — so it can meet tight limits without exhaust after-treatment.

Removing heat with a circulating fluid rather than moving air. In battery containers it holds the temperature spread between cells much tighter than air cooling, which matters because the hottest cell in a string sets the ageing rate for all of them.

A coolant distribution unit that rejects the racks' heat into the room air through a radiator and fans instead of into facility water, so liquid-cooled racks can go into a hall that has no water near them. It pays a much higher approach temperature and fan power, and the room's air system must still carry the heat away.

A pre-agreed sum a contractor or supplier pays per day of delay or per unit of performance shortfall, written into the contract so the owner does not have to prove its loss. Capped in practice, so the independent engineer checks whether the cap actually covers the lender's exposure.

A contractual right for preferred shareholders to be paid a set amount — often a multiple of what they invested — before ordinary shareholders receive anything in a sale or wind-up. A 1.3x preference means the holder takes 1.3 times its money off the top.

A separately stock-exchange-listed company that an asset manager controls or manages, holding a slice of the same assets its private funds hold. It gives the manager permanent capital and gives public investors access to private assets.

An isolated converter that uses a resonant tank so its switches turn on when the voltage across them is already near zero. That removes most of the switching loss and lets the stage run at high frequency, which is how a kilowatt supply fits in a small box.

A pool of capital at Lloyd's of London that underwrites risks through a managing agent for one year at a time. Syndicates participate on layers of large placements and, through coverholders, delegate authority to agents such as renewables MGAs.

Lithium manganese iron phosphate: lithium iron phosphate with manganese added to raise cell voltage and so energy density, while keeping most of the cost and stability advantages. It sits between standard iron-phosphate and nickel chemistries.

Liquefied natural gas: gas cooled until it condenses, shrinking it several hundredfold so far more energy fits in a trailer than compressed gas allows. It needs cryogenic handling and equipment on site to return it to gas, and is used where a site's demand outruns what compressed deliveries can sustain.
A bank of resistors that turns electricity into heat on demand, used to load generators, UPS and batteries during testing when there is no real IT load to use.

Average demand divided by peak demand over a period. A data center running at 90 percent or more is the flattest load a utility serves; a house at 30 percent peaks for a few hours a day. Flat loads use the wires and plants built for them almost all the time, which is why tariffs single them out.

The obligation to supply exactly what customers happen to use, hour by hour, rather than a flat block. A retail supplier is load-following by definition, which is why its purchasing problem is a shape problem and not just a volume one.

The projection of future peak demand and energy that a utility's plan and a grid operator's markets are built on. Data-center requests inflated these forecasts faster than anything in the industry's history, and the arguments — how much of the queue is real, whether the same campus is counted by several utilities — are arguments about this number.
A utility or retail supplier responsible for procuring electricity and capacity for the end customers it serves; in California the buyers of most long-term solar and storage contracts.

Dropping pre-ranked non-critical loads — chillers, offices, lower-priority halls — when generation cannot carry everything, so the critical load keeps its power. The priority list is written in advance and executed automatically by the paralleling controls; it is the reason an under-strength generator fleet degrades gracefully instead of tripping.

A sudden change in the current a load draws — a processor jumping from idle to full work in microseconds. The converter must hold the voltage through it, and how fast it responds, and how much stored charge sits beside the chip to cover the gap, is a central design constraint.
One of ERCOT's four settlement regions (North, South, West, Houston) whose average price loads are charged. A fleet spread across all four earns whichever zone is stressed on a given day.

A government promise to repay a project's lenders if the project cannot. The DOE Loan Programs Office offers them for large energy projects; the guarantee lowers the interest rate because the lender's risk becomes the government's.

Spreading a large loan across several banks, one of which arranges it and one of which administers it. Data-center construction loans of USD 1–2 billion are syndicated because no single bank wants the whole exposure.

Debt as a share of a project's total cost. A bond of USD 4.6 billion against a campus built for about that much is near 100% loan-to-cost: efficient for the sponsor, whose equity is repaid from the proceeds, and fragile for the bondholders, who own any overrun or delay.

A loan's size as a percentage of the collateral backing it. A 50% loan-to-value means the collateral could halve before the lender is exposed — the standard measure of how much cushion a secured loan has.

The wholesale electricity price at one specific point on the grid, equal to the cost of serving one more unit of demand there — energy cost plus the cost of congestion and losses in getting it to that point. Two projects a short distance apart can face very different prices when the transmission between them is full.
A bank account controlled by lenders into which a tenant's rent is paid before anyone else can touch it. It turns a lease into collateral: the cash flow is captured at source rather than promised.

Storage that can discharge for ten hours or more — iron-air, flow batteries, pumped hydro — as opposed to the two- to four-hour lithium-ion plants that make up nearly all of today's grid storage. It targets multi-day gaps in wind and solar rather than the evening peak, and it is still mostly at pilot scale.
Equipment whose manufacturing time is long enough that it must be ordered before the design around it is complete. Transformers, switchgear and chillers are the classic three.
Claims paid divided by premium earned over a period — the underwriter's report card. A book with a loss ratio persistently above what the carrier priced for loses its capacity at renewal.

The chronic plant failure in which return water comes back too cool, so the plant must move far more water for the same cooling and stages on chillers it does not need. Almost always caused downstream, at coils and valves, not at the chiller.

A number format that stores each value in eight bits instead of the sixteen or thirty-two once used, with FP4 halving it again. Neural networks tolerate the lost precision surprisingly well, so each generation of lower-precision arithmetic roughly doubles the throughput and halves the memory a model needs — which is why headline performance figures are meaningless without the format they were measured in.

A refrigerant whose cycle runs below atmospheric pressure on the low side, so a leak draws air in rather than pushing refrigerant out. It permits a very different, thinner-walled machine and needs a purge unit.

Utilization-level voltage — under about a thousand volts, the 400 or 480 V that feeds distribution boards, UPS units and the racks. Most UPS equipment has historically lived here; moving it up to medium voltage is one of the live arguments in gigawatt campuses.

The requirement to keep operating through a dip in supply voltage rather than disconnecting, specified as a curve of how deep a dip must be survived for how long. The demanding case — a fall to near zero for a few cycles while protection clears a fault — can only be met with stored energy, because for those cycles almost nothing is arriving.

Long-term service agreement: the multi-year operations-and-maintenance contract through which a supplier delivers availability guarantees on the equipment it sold. Suppliers generally will not extend long-dated warranties without holding it, so the LTSA and the warranty are negotiated as one package.
A fixed price for a fully defined scope, bid competitively. Cheapest where the design is complete and most expensive where it is not, because every change becomes a negotiation.

A construction contract in which one party delivers a complete working plant for one fixed price on one fixed date, holding the design, the procurement and the building. What the owner is really buying is certainty: the contractor replaces a distribution of possible costs with a single number and absorbs the tail, and the premium over expected cost is what that transfer costs.

A bearing that holds a shaft in place with controlled magnetic fields instead of contact, so a high-speed flywheel can spin with almost no friction and no lubrication. It is what lets a small, light rotor store useful energy at tens of thousands of rpm — and it needs control power of its own.

A switchgear arrangement with two incoming supplies, each feeding half the bus, and a normally-open tie breaker between them. Lose one supply and the tie closes so the surviving source carries everything, which is why each source must be sized for the whole load. It is the standard way a campus takes two utility feeds and the reason a one-line drawing has to be read for what happens after the tie closes, not just before.

An air-permitting classification for a plant whose potential emissions exceed the thresholds that trigger full pre-construction review — modelling, public comment and best-available-control analysis. Crossing the line turns a permit measured in months into one measured in years, so on-site plants are packaged to stay under it.
Water added to a cooling or process loop to replace what evaporation, blowdown and leakage remove. A site's water demand is largely its makeup rate.
The annual fee a fund manager charges investors on committed or invested capital — typically 1–2% — to run the firm regardless of performance.

A specialist underwriting agency that prices and binds insurance on a carrier's paper under delegated authority, paid by commission and sometimes a profit share, and holding no insurance risk on its own balance sheet. It sells expertise the carrier does not want to staff.

In a limited liability company, the member that runs the business day to day and makes operating decisions, regardless of how much of the economic ownership it holds. Invenergy's management is managing member with CDPQ and Blackstone as majority economic owners.

A per-connection factor applied to every megawatt-hour a plant sells, scaling its output for the losses between where it connects and the reference point where prices are set. Used in the Australian market and recalculated periodically, so a revision can move a plant's revenue by several per cent with nothing having changed at the plant.

Restating an open contract at today's market price so that unrealised gains and losses appear in the accounts immediately. It makes a hedged generator's reported earnings swing with prices even when the underlying physical business has not changed.

Quoting a price to buy and a price to sell the same asset continuously, and earning the difference. The market maker supplies liquidity and takes inventory risk; it does not need the price to go up to make money.

Revenue that depends on trading, transaction volumes or market conditions, and therefore swings year to year. A firm's mix of annuity-style and markets-facing income is a summary of how volatile its earnings should be.
Reshaping an entire site to the elevations the design needs, before any building work. It is the first major scope on a greenfield project and the least reversible.

A standing set of terms, rates and conditions between an owner and a contractor, against which individual jobs are released without re-tendering each one. It is how repeat buyers actually secure construction capacity — what is competed, once, is the relationship rather than the project.

The standing issuer in a data-center ABS programme: it owns a pool of leased buildings and can add collateral and sell new series of bonds against the pool over time, instead of setting up a new structure for every deal.
A single thick reinforced slab under an entire structure, spreading its load over the whole footprint. Used where soil is weak, loads are heavy, or differential settlement must be controlled.

A US test that asks what share of a project's or component's direct costs did NOT come from a restricted foreign supplier. The share must exceed a threshold that rises each year, so it is a sliding cost calculation rather than a list of banned companies.
Distribution-level voltage, roughly the single-digit to tens of kilovolts — the tier data centers and storage plants connect at before power is stepped down to usable levels.
A written statement of shared intentions between parties, typically governments and companies, that commits neither to spend money. Gigawatt-scale AI announcements at summits are often MoUs.

How fast data can be moved between a processor and its memory, usually quoted in terabytes per second. For most AI work the arithmetic units finish faster than memory can supply them, so bandwidth rather than raw compute sets the achieved speed.

Mechanical, electrical and plumbing — the building services trades taken together. On a data-centre schedule MEP is where most of the labour hours and most of the risk sit, which is why who holds those trades decides who can compress the programme.
A power project with no long-term contract: it sells into the wholesale market at whatever prices turn out to be. Higher upside, no floor — which is why lenders ask what else backs the debt.

A transmission line built by a private developer that earns its money from customers who buy capacity on it — under a FERC tariff — rather than from a utility's regulated rate base. Grain Belt Express is one; its risk is that customers must be found before the line is financed.

The ranking of generators by the cost of producing their next unit of electricity, cheapest first. The grid operator works down the list until demand is met, and the last unit needed usually sets the price everyone is paid.

The most rigorously defined class of medium-voltage switchgear (IEEE C37.20.2): draw-out breakers, grounded metal barriers between every major compartment, insulated bus, and shutters that cover the live stabs when a breaker is withdrawn. The compartmentalisation is the point — it limits how far a fault inside one cell can propagate and lets a breaker be pulled with the bus alive.
Fuel in the form of a uranium alloy rather than a ceramic oxide pellet. It conducts heat far better, runs cooler, and expands when hot in a way that helps shut the reaction down.

A gaseous fuel's resistance to knock, the equivalent of octane rating for liquid fuels. Heavier hydrocarbons lower it, and a low-number gas makes a highly-boosted engine detonate — so the controls retard timing and reduce output, and a fuel problem shows up as a capacity shortfall.

A self-contained power system — generation, storage, and controls — that can run connected to the grid or islanded on its own. It is how some AI campuses get power before utility interconnection arrives.
A reactor in the single-digit-to-tens-of-megawatts class, small enough to be transported largely assembled and installed as equipment rather than constructed as a plant.

Investor money released in tranches only when agreed events occur — capacity delivered, targets hit — rather than all at signing. It ties a strategic investor's cash to its own or a partner's performance.

A US law requiring contractors on federal construction projects to post payment and performance bonds, so subcontractors and suppliers have a surety to claim against if they are not paid. Because bonds are public, the resulting court records reveal which sureties back a private contractor.

A construction-plus-a-few-years loan that must be refinanced after a short term (often five to seven years) rather than amortising over the asset's life. Hedges and puts that lift debt 'during the mini-perm period' are sized to that first refinancing.

A tariff term that bills a large customer for a fixed share of its contracted capacity every month whether or not it draws it — the utility's version of take-or-pay. It converts a speculative interconnection request into demand the utility can finance plant against, and it is what makes a phased campus pay for megawatts it has not energized yet.

The lowest output a machine can hold continuously without cycling off. A centrifugal chiller's floor is set by surge, and a plant that spends the year below its smallest machine's floor is a plant that was staged wrong.

An air-permitting category for a plant whose potential emissions sit below the major-source thresholds, sometimes by accepting enforceable limits on hours or fuel — a synthetic minor. It replaces months of modelling and public comment with a far lighter permit, which is why on-site power blocks are sized to fit beneath the line.

The share of a subsidiary's earnings that belongs to an outside investor rather than to the parent's shareholders. Selling a minority stake raises cash without issuing shares, and the price is a permanent deduction from reported earnings — which is why a utility's earnings can fall in a year its business grew.

The Midcontinent Independent System Operator — the RTO for fifteen central US states and Manitoba. Its South region, added in 2013, covers Louisiana, Arkansas, Mississippi and the Texas Gulf coast, so Entergy's operating companies buy and sell wholesale power, get their capacity accredited and have their big lines planned there rather than in ERCOT or PJM.

Generating sets packaged on trailers and paralleled through switchgear trailers, so a plant can be assembled at one site and moved to the next. It costs more per megawatt-hour than fixed plant because transport limits sacrifice efficiency, heat rejection and acoustics — and it is worth more at the end of a job, because the equipment has somewhere else to go.

A transformer, switchgear and protection package built onto trailers so it can be delivered and energised in weeks. Bought as insurance against a failure, or as a schedule instrument when the permanent substation is late.

A long-established, deliberately simple industrial communication protocol used to read measurements from and send commands to equipment. Its ubiquity is the point: a plant that speaks it can be monitored and dispatched by almost anyone's software, which is why owners ask for it at a system's boundary.

Building a model by repeatedly showing it data and adjusting its internal parameters. It is one very long job spread across thousands of accelerators that must stay synchronised, which is why it drives demand for the fastest interconnect and the densest racks.

A light material — water, graphite — that slows fast fission neutrons down to thermal speeds, where they are far more likely to cause the next fission. Removing the moderator is what makes a reactor a fast reactor.

A lease in which rent covers some operating costs and the tenant pays others directly — between a gross lease (everything in the rent) and a triple-net lease (tenant pays everything). Which costs sit where decides who bears the risk of rising power and insurance bills.

A storage architecture built from several smaller self-contained units rather than one large container. Each unit is lighter to transport and fails independently, at the cost of repeating the thermal and fire-protection overhead per unit and adding foundations, terminations and commissioning hours.

A UPS built from hot-swappable power modules in a common frame, so capacity is added a module at a time and a failed module is replaced without dropping the load. It trades a slightly higher cost per kilowatt for the ability to buy redundancy and capacity in small increments as a hall fills.
The simplest private-equity scorecard: money out divided by money in. A 3x means the investor got three dollars back for each one put in, regardless of how long it took.

A design in which the coolant, and sometimes the fuel itself, is a molten fluoride or chloride salt. Very high boiling point, low pressure, and a chemistry problem that has to be solved before it is an engineering problem.

An inverter stopping its current injection for the duration of a grid disturbance while staying nominally connected, then resuming when conditions return to range. Harmless on one machine; when a large share of generation does it at once the lost injection resembles the sudden loss of a very large power station, which is why it is now prohibited inside must-ride-through zones.
A fixed monthly charge for an amount of compute regardless of use — the cloud equivalent of rent. Paired with a short termination notice it is flexible for the buyer and fragile for the seller.

Metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor: a switch in which a voltage on an insulated gate opens or closes a conducting channel. It conducts with electrons only, so it stops conducting the instant the gate is pulled low and behaves like a resistor when on.
A contract term guaranteeing one customer terms at least as good as any later customer receives, sometimes with a payment if the seller later achieves lower costs.

Mean time between failures: the average running time between one failure and the next across a population of a device, calculated from its parts count or from field data. It is a statement about a fleet rather than a promise about one unit, and it says nothing about how long the repair takes — which is why availability also needs the mean time to repair.

The MISO Transmission Expansion Plan — the RTO's yearly regional transmission plan, the MISO counterpart of PJM's RTEP. Big lines are approved here and their cost allocated across the footprint, on a horizon of five to fifteen years.

A delivery model in which the owner lets several direct contracts — civil, electrical, substation, commissioning — instead of one wrapped contract, and coordinates them itself. It avoids the wrap premium and keeps every seam between the scopes, so what the owner saves in price it pays in coordination and in delay arguments it must referee rather than transfer.

A compute buyer's deliberate use of more than one kind of AI accelerator — for example NVIDIA GPUs, Google TPUs and Amazon Trainium — so that no single supplier's allocation, price or roadmap can stall it. Costs more engineering; buys leverage.

A rate case that sets rates for several years at once, with pre-approved step increases as a capital plan is built, instead of a new case each time. It gives the utility certainty on recovery and the commission a settled bill trajectory; Minnesota and Colorado use it, and it is the instrument through which a large capital plan lands on customers on a schedule.

A point-of-load converter built from several identical stages that take turns delivering current into one output. Splitting the job spreads the heat, shrinks the filter each stage needs, and lets the controller shut stages off at light load.

Making money by selling a business at a higher valuation ratio than you paid, without the business itself changing much. The alternative to growing earnings, and the one most dependent on market timing.

A contractual or market requirement that a resource make its capability available to the system operator whenever it is physically able, rather than choosing to sit out. It is what makes a capacity payment meaningful: the buyer is paying for the certainty of being able to call on the resource.

The planning rule that a network must survive losing any single element without shedding load. It is why transmission looks over-built on a normal day, and why one outage can make a region's apparent spare capacity vanish at once.

Redundancy shorthand: N is the equipment needed to carry the load, N+1 adds one spare unit, 2N doubles everything. Data centers price reliability in these terms — more redundancy means fewer outages and more capital.

The maximum output a generator is rated to produce under ideal conditions, stamped on the machine. It is not what the resource contributes to meeting peak demand: a 100 MW nameplate solar farm may be credited with a fraction of that in a planning study. Portfolio announcements are usually stated in nameplate, and accredited or effective capacity is the smaller number that actually counts.
Fluid moving through a loop because hot fluid is less dense than cold, with no pump. A reactor that can remove decay heat this way keeps cooling itself after losing all electrical power.

An offset that comes from owning two businesses whose exposures point in opposite directions, rather than from buying a financial contract. A company that both generates electricity and sells it to retail customers is long supply and short demand at the same time, so a price move that hurts one side helps the other.

A US defense-authorization provision restricting Department of Defense battery procurement from named Chinese suppliers — the list that made "is your cell maker §154-listed?" a standard sourcing question.
Sealing a work area and holding it at slightly lower pressure than its surroundings, with filtered exhaust, so dust and contaminants flow inward rather than out into the live space.
A core designed so that getting hotter makes the chain reaction weaker. Power then self-corrects without any operator or control system acting — the physical basis of a passive-safety claim.

The North American convention for describing what an electrical enclosure keeps out, covering dust and water plus ice, corrosion and outdoor exposure. It overlaps the international ingress-protection scale without mapping onto it cleanly, and officials tend to ask for whichever one their adopted code cites.
A newer GPU-cloud provider renting AI compute capacity, typically growing faster than its capital base — a distinct buyer class from the hyperscalers.

The North American Electric Reliability Corporation: the body that writes and enforces the mandatory reliability standards for the bulk power system, including the ride-through and disturbance-monitoring requirements that apply to transmission-connected inverter-based resources.

Performance fees a manager has earned on paper because its investments have risen in value, but has not yet collected because the assets have not been sold. It reverses if values fall before the exit.

What a firm's assets are worth after subtracting what it owes. For a trading and investing business it is the most meaningful measure of size, because revenue can be enormous while the capital at risk is small, or the reverse.

A lease under which the tenant, not the landlord, pays the property's operating costs — taxes, insurance and maintenance. A triple-net lease passes all three, which makes the landlord's rent unusually predictable.

How much more electricity a company has committed to sell than it can produce, or the reverse, over a given period. Being long means owning output with no buyer yet; being short means owing power that has not been secured.
A management-accounting figure showing what each division earned before group-level costs, staff profit share and tax. Divisional figures added together will not equal group profit, by design.

The megawatts a resource is allowed to count toward a resource-adequacy obligation, after the system operator discounts its nameplate rating for how reliably it can deliver during the hours that matter. For storage the discount depends heavily on how many hours it can run at full output.

A number the bitcoin network adjusts so that blocks keep arriving about every ten minutes no matter how much hashrate joins or leaves. If total hashrate doubles, difficulty roughly doubles, and each machine's share of the rewards roughly halves.

Transmission equipment — new lines, larger transformers, reconductored circuits — that the grid needs before a new project can connect without overloading something. The interconnection study assigns their cost to the project, and that assignment is often what decides whether the project is built.
The effective target area a nucleus presents to a neutron, measured in barns. It is strongly energy-dependent, which is why slowing a neutron down changes what it will do.

The US standard for emergency and standby power systems. It classes a system by how fast it must pick up the load after the normal supply fails — the usual data-center class must be carrying load within ten seconds — and by how long it must be able to run, and it sets the testing and maintenance regime that keeps a backup plant honest.

The US standard for deflagration venting — giving an explosion a deliberate, engineered escape route so pressure is released where it does least harm. It is one of the two complementary answers to accumulated flammable gas in an enclosure; the other is preventing the accumulation in the first place.

The US standard for explosion prevention systems — stopping an explosive atmosphere from forming, typically through ventilation, inerting or gas detection. It is the complement to venting: one removes the cause, the other manages the consequence.

The US standard for electrical safety in the workplace: it requires an energised-work justification, an arc-flash risk assessment, labelling of equipment with its incident energy, and protective clothing matched to that number. It governs the people rather than the equipment — the equipment answer to the same hazard is arc-resistant construction.
The US fire-protection standard for stationary energy storage installations — spacing, enclosures, suppression, and the fire testing (UL 9540A) it references. Permitting officials work from it.

Nickel manganese cobalt: a lithium-ion cathode chemistry with higher energy density than LFP but higher cost and more thermal-runaway risk — favored where weight matters, largely displaced by LFP in stationary storage.

The ERCOT rule change setting ride-through obligations for inverter-based resources, battery storage included. It is the resource-side counterpart to NOGRR 282, which governs large electronic loads: adjacent numbers, opposite sides of the same interface, and confusing the two is a common and expensive error in a technical room.

The ERCOT rule requiring new large electronic loads — data centers of 75 MW and up — to ride through voltage and frequency disturbances instead of tripping off together. It is a load rule rather than a storage standard (those are NOGRR 245 and 272), and it is what makes buffering between the grid and the GPUs close to mandatory in Texas.

Net operating income: a property's rental income minus the direct costs of operating it, before interest, tax, depreciation and corporate overhead. It is the number that gets divided by a cap rate to value a building.

A region where outdoor air already fails a federal ambient standard for a pollutant such as ozone or fine particulates. Adding a combustion source there faces the strictest review and offset requirements, so low-emission machines can site where diesel and open-flame plants cannot.
A letter of intent, memorandum or master agreement that expresses intent to transact without obligating either party to do so. In a pre-revenue pipeline it is a marker of interest, not of a sale.

Standby capability that is not already running but can be started and delivering within a defined short window, typically minutes, if a generator trips or demand surges. Batteries qualify easily because they need no warm-up, so the service is nearly free revenue while they sit idle.

A real-estate investment trust sold to individual investors that is not listed on a stock exchange. Investors get their money back by asking the fund to buy their shares, not by selling to another investor — which works until too many ask at once.

Using a resource such as a battery, sited at a constrained point on the network, to defer or avoid building a new line or substation. The utility buys a service that relieves the constraint instead of buying steel and copper.

Nitrogen oxides: the pollutant family formed when the air's own nitrogen burns at high flame temperature. It drives ozone formation downwind and is the number most air permits are written around — which is why diesels carry after-treatment, gas engines run lean and turbines carry low-NOx combustors.

New product introduction — the phase between a working prototype and volume production, where the design is made buildable: tooling cut, test fixtures written, the line laid out and the first units built and torn down. It is where most of a manufacturing relationship's risk actually sits.

Non-standard part-load value: the same weighted part-load calculation as IPLV but computed at the temperatures the actual project will run at. It is the honest number when the design is not the standard rating point.

A laboratory formally recognised in the United States to test and certify products against safety standards. Its mark on equipment is what a listing means in practice, and its ongoing factory surveillance is why a listing certifies a production process rather than a prototype.

The projected cost of a unit built after the design, the supply chain and the workforce have repeated it enough times to stop improving. Every modular-reactor economic case is a claim about how fast the curve between the first and the nth actually falls.
The formal instruction to the contractor to start building, given once financing, permits and equipment are in place. It is the moment a development project becomes a construction project.

Raising an existing reactor's licensed output — by a few percent through better instrumentation, or by up to a fifth through new turbines and equipment — with the regulator's approval. It is the cheapest firm capacity a utility with a nuclear fleet can add, because the site, the licence and the operators already exist.

The independent system operator for New York State, which runs the state's wholesale energy, ancillary-service and installed-capacity markets. It is divided into zones whose prices diverge sharply because the transmission linking upstate generation to downstate load is limited.

Operations and maintenance: the contract to run and maintain a plant, usually long-dated and usually renewed. A builder that sells a completed plant but keeps this contract converts a one-off construction margin into recurring revenue, keeps its crews employed between builds, and accumulates the operating record the next customer wants to inspect.

A component going out of production while the product that uses it is still selling. Managing it — last-time buys, qualified replacements, redesign — is a standing cost of owning any electronic product for more than a few years.

Original design manufacturer — a firm that designs the product as well as building it, then sells it to a brand or a buyer who puts their own label on it. The design, and the ability to sell it again to the next customer, stays with the manufacturer.

The highest price a generator is permitted to bid into a wholesale market. In an energy-only market it also caps the scarcity revenue that is supposed to pay for building new plants, so where the regulator sets it is an investment decision as much as a consumer-protection one.

The schedule a resource submits to the market saying how much it will sell or buy at each price. For a battery the curve encodes a decision about the future — selling now forfeits the ability to sell later — so building it is a forecasting problem, not a cost calculation.

A federal seabed lease auctioned by the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management that gives a developer the exclusive right to study and, with later permits, build wind turbines in an area. Buying the lease is the first and cheapest step; Invenergy's four cost USD 765 million and were bought back at that price.

Building the electrical rooms, power centres and cooling modules in a factory and shipping them as tested blocks, so site work shrinks to foundations, steel and connections. The developer's tool for making the delivery date credible.
The committed purchase of a project's output — power, capacity, or storage services. Signed offtake is what turns a development pipeline into a financeable project.
The buyer that has agreed to purchase a project's output — electricity, steam or capacity — under a long-term contract; the credit the lenders look through to.

A switch inside a transformer that changes the number of turns in use — and so the output voltage — without interrupting the load. It is the only substantial moving part in most transformers, which makes it the part most likely to need maintenance and one of the more common causes of transformer outages.

The resistance a switch shows while it is conducting, written R-DS(on). Multiply it by the square of the current to get the heat the device makes just by being on. It rises with temperature, so a hot device wastes more than a cold one carrying the same current.
Using fuel once and then storing it, which is what the United States does. Recycling changes the volume and the heat load of what is left, and does not remove the need to store something.

A modern industrial communication standard in which devices describe their own data — what each value means, its units and its type — rather than exposing bare numbered registers. It is more secure and self-documenting than older protocols, which is why newer control systems offer it alongside them rather than instead of them.
The FERC-approved rate schedule under which a transmission owner must let anyone buy capacity on its line on published terms. A merchant line needs one before it can sell service.

The voltage a cell settles to when it is resting with no current flowing, which maps to how full it is. It gives an absolute reading where charge counting only gives an accumulating one, but the cell must genuinely rest first — and for the flat-voltage chemistries common in grid storage a tiny voltage difference stands for a large difference in charge.

An industry body through which operators and vendors publish hardware designs — rack dimensions, power distribution, cooling interfaces — as open specifications. Contributing a design there is how a vendor invites others to build compatible parts, and how a buyer avoids being locked to one supplier's mechanical and electrical choices.

A transfer that opens the old source before closing onto the new one — break-before-make — so for a moment the load is fed by nothing. Simpler, and it never back-feeds the utility, but the gap means the UPS or some other stored energy has to carry the load across it or the servers see an outage.
A lease the landlord keeps on its own balance sheet as property, recognising rent evenly over the term. The building stays the landlord's asset and the tenant simply pays for use.
A specification that names a product and permits alternatives judged equivalent. It is the clause by which a second and third vendor get into a bid — and the clause all three of them argue about.

The reactors, units or capacity a vendor counts as sold or reserved; the word covers everything from signed purchase orders to non-binding options, so the terms behind the number matter more than the number.

Revenue growth stripped of acquisitions, disposals and currency — what the existing business did on its own. For brokers it is the single most-watched number, because acquisitions can buy revenue indefinitely and organic growth cannot be bought.

The developer that finds the site, secures the land and grid position, wins the contract and carries the project to a saleable stage — and then may sell rather than build and own. Its product is a de-risked project, not electricity.

Joining two or more sources to one bus through devices that let current flow only out of each source — an OR gate for power. A source that fails or is unplugged cannot drag the bus down or draw current from its neighbours, which is what makes redundant supplies and live swaps safe.

Changing a deployed product's software remotely across an installed fleet. It is how control software keeps improving after installation, and it is also a compliance risk: a product is certified as configured, so an update touching protection behaviour changes the safety case and has to pass through formal change control.

How much more than its nameplate a UPS will carry and for how long — commonly a few tens of percent for minutes, and a large multiple for a fraction of a second. It is what lets a downstream breaker clear a fault instead of the inverter folding back and the whole bus collapsing.

Installing more capacity than a contract requires on day one, so that natural degradation never carries the plant below its guaranteed floor. It is the simplest way to keep a long capacity promise and the least efficient use of capital, since the surplus is bought at day-one prices and sits idle for years.

Major equipment bought by the project owner directly from the manufacturer and handed to a contractor to install, test and connect. It is the norm in grid storage because the supply agreement, the capacity guarantee and the tax position work better held by the owner — and it means a late or damaged delivery is the owner's delay rather than the contractor's.

The engineering firm an owner hires to act as its technical agent — writing the specification, reviewing the contractor's design submittals, witnessing tests and advising on change orders — as distinct from the contractor's engineer of record or the lender's independent engineer. Paid a fee; takes no equity and builds nothing.

An exhaust device that finishes burning the carbon monoxide and unburned hydrocarbons an engine left behind, turning them into carbon dioxide and water. It costs a little efficiency through backpressure and is poisoned over time by contaminants in fuel and lubricating oil.

Restating an exhaust concentration at a standard oxygen level so that diluting the exhaust with air cannot make a source look cleaner than it is. A parts-per-million emissions figure quoted without its reference oxygen level is not a measurement that can be compared with anything.

The output level a wind or solar plant is expected to exceed half the time — the central estimate a forecast and a financing are built on. A year at 87% of P-50 means the wind simply blew less than the median expectation, which is a revenue miss no contract protects against.

The output level a wind or solar plant is expected to exceed 99 years in 100 — the deep downside case a lender sizes debt to when it wants near-certainty. A parametric hedge that adds cash flow above the P99 wind speed raises the floor the lender counts.

A dividend or interest payment settled by increasing the amount owed rather than by paying cash. It preserves cash today at the cost of a claim that compounds, so a paid-in-kind preferred stake grows its share of the company for as long as it goes unpaid.

A corporation created alongside a partnership so that its shares are economically identical to the partnership's units and exchangeable one for one. It exists to let investors who cannot or will not hold partnership units buy the same economics.

Switchgear whose controller synchronizes several generators onto one common bus, adds them in a set order, shares the load between them and sheds low-priority load if generation runs short — a room of engines behaving as one plant. It is what turns a collection of standby gen-sets into a campus-scale power source.

Cover that pays a pre-agreed amount when a measured index — wind speed, rainfall, an earthquake magnitude — crosses a threshold, rather than reimbursing an adjusted loss. Fast and objective, but it carries basis risk: the index can trigger without a loss, or a loss can occur without the index moving.

The measured index that decides whether a parametric policy pays — a wind speed at a station, a hail-stone diameter, an earthquake magnitude. Choosing it is the whole design problem: a tight trigger pays reliably and costs more, a loose one is cheap and may not pay when the damage is real.

The unwanted inductance of the wiring, leadframe and copper around a switch. It resists sudden changes in current, so it turns a fast turn-off into a voltage spike across the device — which is why package design, not silicon, often sets how fast a converter is allowed to switch.

The energy a storage system consumes to keep itself alive — cooling, pumps, fans, controls and heating. It comes straight out of delivered round-trip efficiency, it is the line an enclosure designer most directly controls, and it moves sharply with climate, which is why efficiency figures are only comparable at stated conditions.

A promise by a larger corporate parent to stand behind a subsidiary's contractual obligations, so the buyer's effective counterparty becomes the parent. It is only as strong as that parent and only as broad as its wording — a guarantee capped at contract value may not reach the loss a buyer actually fears.

The NRC's two-step licensing path for a power reactor: a construction permit to build, then an operating licence to run — as opposed to Part 52, which combines design certification, site and construction into one combined licence.

The technology-inclusive, risk-informed US licensing framework written for reactors that are not large light-water plants, so that a design need not be argued against rules drafted for something else.

Running a generating machine below its full rating. Efficiency and emissions both move with load — a large gas turbine is efficient only near full output, while a fleet of engines can shut units down and keep the rest at their sweet spot — so the shape of the load, not just its peak, decides which machine is cheaper to run.
Duty in which a battery is cycled without ever being returned to full. It is normal in solar, telecom and grid work, and it is precisely the condition ordinary lead-acid tolerates worst.

Fine solid and liquid particles in exhaust, regulated by size because the smallest travel deepest into the lungs. Diesel engines produce enough to need a filter; gas engines produce very little, which is a large part of why gas displaces diesel wherever a machine will run many hours.

The usual tax-equity structure: the investor holds most of the partnership's tax benefits and some cash until it reaches a target return, then its share 'flips' down to a small residual and the developer keeps the rest. A hybrid flip mixes this with a credit transfer.

Operating costs the landlord incurs and bills straight to the tenant — power, water, taxes, insurance — without markup. In a backstopped lease the guarantor often covers pass-throughs as well as base rent.

The build-up of an oxide or hydroxide layer on an electrode that blocks further reaction. In iron batteries it thickens with cycling, raising internal resistance and gradually cutting the capacity and power the cell can deliver.

Safety that rests on physics and geometry rather than on pumps, valves and operator action — gravity, natural circulation, thermal expansion. The claim is only as good as the conditions under which it was demonstrated.
Printed circuit board assembly — a bare board with its components soldered on and tested. It is the unit most electronics manufacturing is priced and scheduled in, one level below a finished product.

Power conversion system: the bidirectional inverter of a battery plant — converts the batteries' DC to grid AC when discharging and back when charging. Its rating sets the plant's power (MW), while the batteries set its energy (MWh).

Power delivery network: everything between a converter's output and the transistors on the chip — board copper, package pins, vias, the substrate and the decoupling capacitors along the way. Its resistance and inductance set how much voltage is lost on the way and how fast the supply can answer a transient.
Power distribution unit: data-center gear that splits and distributes power to the racks — the branch circuits between the UPS and the servers.

Running on-site generation or storage during the hours that set a site's demand charge, so the meter never records the peak. It turns a backup asset into an earning one, but it also moves the engine out of the emergency-only regulatory class and into a permit that counts its hours.

A gas-cooled reactor whose fuel is thousands of billiard-ball-sized graphite spheres, each packed with TRISO particles, that flow slowly down through the core and are refuelled continuously while the reactor runs.

A right to buy shares at a nominal price (often USD 0.01), so its value is almost the full share price. Given to a guarantor or lender, it is equity compensation for credit support — the price of a backstop paid in the company's own stock.
A pool of retirement savings that invests for decades and prizes steady, inflation-linked cash flow — which is why pension funds like CDPQ own infrastructure and renewable developers directly.
The share of a portfolio's capacity or revenue covered by long-term contracts. It is the first number an infrastructure fund asks for, because it sets how much debt the portfolio can carry.

Useful work divided by the power it took. Once a site's electrical supply is fixed, this is the number that decides how much computing the site can ever contain, which is why it matters more to a data-centre buyer than peak performance does.

A solar plant's measured output divided by the output the sunlight actually available should have produced, after correcting for temperature. Expressed as a percentage; the most widely used single measure of whether a solar plant is healthy.

Investment money with no fixed date on which it must be returned — the opposite of a closed-end fund. At asset level it means a sponsor buying into specific stabilized campuses and committing to future ones without a change of control or a sale.

A fund with no fixed end date, so it never has to sell an asset to return capital to investors. The opposite of a closed-end fund with a ten-year life, and the reason two owners of similar assets can face completely different pressure to exit.

A stage at the front of an AC supply that forces the current it draws to follow the shape of the mains voltage. Without it the supply draws current in short peaks, which wastes capacity in every transformer and cable upstream and is limited by standards.

The standard rack-side coolant: inhibited propylene glycol mixed 25 percent by volume with deionised or filtered water. The glycol carries the corrosion-inhibitor package, protects to about −10 °C and suppresses microbial growth; 25 percent is the least that does all three without costing much of the water's heat capacity.

A cash promise equal to what a share would be worth, granted without issuing the share, so an employee gains from a sale or valuation event while the founder's cap table stays clean. Its weakness is that its value is whatever the company's own valuation says — the substance of the 2026 suits against Prime.
