The control circuit inside a grid-following inverter that continuously estimates the grid voltage's frequency and phase so the machine can synchronise its injected current to them. It needs a firm voltage to lock onto, which is why grid-following inverters struggle where system strength is low.

A driven pile stopping short of its design depth against rock, cobbles or a dense layer. It converts a fast, cheap operation into a pre-drilled or drilled one at whatever fraction of locations is affected — and establishing that fraction in advance is exactly what the geotechnical investigation was for.

The largest US regional grid operator, spanning the mid-Atlantic and parts of the Midwest — including northern Virginia's data-center corridor. Its capacity market and interconnection queue shape much of the AI data-center power story.

The act of getting a risk covered: marketing the submission, collecting quotes, structuring the layers, allocating shares among insurers and binding. A programme is 'placed' when every layer is full — and a layer that cannot be filled is where a project's financing stalls.

A court-approved corporate reorganisation used in Canada to restructure share ownership between related companies. It is how a parent can move a business into a listed subsidiary in exchange for newly issued shares.

A zoning approval that treats a large site as one negotiated plan — uses, heights, setbacks, phasing, community obligations — instead of applying the standard district rules lot by lot. The instrument under which a multi-building campus is approved.

The cushion of accredited capacity a system must hold above its forecast peak — typically 15 to 25 percent — so that outages, weather and forecast error do not produce shortfalls. A rising load forecast raises the megawatts the margin requires; the margin, not the peak, is what a utility certifies plants against.

A stack of thin corrugated metal plates through which two fluids flow in alternate channels, so heat crosses the metal while the fluids never mix. It is the boundary inside a liquid-to-liquid CDU between facility water and rack coolant; more plate area buys a lower approach temperature.

Growing an acquired business by building far more of what it already does, rather than by improving its margins or reselling it at a higher multiple. It is the value-creation route that takes the longest and shows up as capacity growth.
A fund's investment in an operating company that then buys or develops many projects, rather than in one project at a time; the platform carries the team and pipeline, the fund carries the capital.

Selling the whole developer — its projects at every stage, its pipeline, land and queue positions, and its team — rather than one project. The buyer pays for the machine that makes projects, not just the projects.
A concentrated load applied over a small area — a rack foot, a jack, a transformer wheel. A floor can satisfy a uniform load rating and still fail a point-load check under the same equipment.

The translation table that says which numeric register on a particular make and model of equipment holds which measurement, and how to scale it. Every manufacturer arranges these differently, so a monitoring platform needs one per device type — an unglamorous library that is difficult to reproduce and therefore commercially valuable.
The exact physical place where a customer's or a generator's equipment meets the utility's. Every study, tariff, protection setting and argument about who pays refers back to it.

The final converter in the chain, placed as close as physically possible to the device it feeds, so that the very large current at a very low voltage travels only millimetres. Everything upstream can run at a higher voltage; the point of load is where the chain gives that up.

A transmission charge spread evenly across every customer in a region regardless of where the line was built — the same price to send a letter anywhere. ERCOT allocates its transmission cost of service this way across all load, which is why a 765 kV line in West Texas is paid for by customers in Dallas and Houston, and why Texas has built transmission faster than regions that argue about who benefits.

What a plant could emit running at maximum capacity every hour of the year, unless its permit contains enforceable limits saying otherwise. It is a ceiling rather than a forecast, and comparing it with the applicable thresholds is what sorts a project into a light permit or a multi-year review.

A battery optimized for how fast it can deliver rather than how much it holds — sized by discharge rate against a short duration, and judged on rate capability and on how well it survives sitting fully charged. A backup-supply battery is the archetype, and its design choices run opposite to an energy battery's at almost every point.
The rule that a site must have firm electricity — reserved grid capacity or on-site generation — before accelerators are worth ordering, because chips can be bought in months and power takes years.

Cleaning up the supply before it reaches the load — holding voltage and frequency steady, removing harmonics, riding through sags and spikes — as distinct from replacing the supply when it fails. Every UPS does some of it; a double-conversion or rotary unit does all of it, all the time.

How much conversion capability fits in a given volume, usually watts per cubic inch or per litre. In racks where every rack unit is contested, a denser converter buys back space for compute — which is why the metric has become a competitive scoreboard.

The ratio of useful power to apparent power — how much of the current a facility draws actually does work. The rest is reactive power: magnetizing current sloshing between source and load, doing nothing but occupying wires and transformers, which is why utilities bill penalties when it runs low.

Choosing a data-center location by where firm electricity can be had soonest — a hydro region with spare generation, a miner's energized substation, a gas microgrid — rather than by proximity to customers or fiber.

The controller responsible for how a plant behaves at its connection point — real and reactive power, voltage and frequency response — as the grid operator requires. It sits above the individual converters and below any market-facing dispatch layer, and it is bound tightly to the interconnection agreement.

A slide-in conversion tray occupying rack units and feeding the rack's own DC busbar, replacing per-server conversion with a pooled stage. Shelves are built with one more module than the load needs, so any single module can fail or be swapped while the rack keeps running.

A factory-assembled block of electrical equipment — transformer, switchgear, distribution and controls — built and tested on a steel frame in a shop and delivered as one unit. It moves work off the construction site and into a factory, which is usually the faster of the two.

A single package holding a half-bridge of switches together with the driver that turns them on and off. Integrating them shortens the connections between driver and switch, which is what lets the pair switch fast enough and cleanly enough to be useful at high current.

A parcel that already has a grid connection or on-site generation secured, sold or leased to a customer who brings the building and the load. In the AI build-out the power is the scarce part, so powered land is priced on megawatts, not acres.

A data-center building delivered with structure, utility power connection and often the substation, but without the tenant's electrical distribution, UPS, generators and cooling. Cheapest rent, most tenant control, longest fit-out — the product a land-and-entitlement developer sells.
Power purchase agreement: a long-term contract to buy a project's power or capacity at agreed terms — the bankable revenue stream that lets developers finance construction.

MISO's Planning Resource Auction — the yearly auction that clears capacity for the coming year, by season and by zone, and sets the price a utility short of its reserve margin pays. MISO's counterpart of PJM's Base Residual Auction, with a one-year rather than three-year horizon.

The North American reliability standard making ride-through mandatory for inverter-based resources, storage included — the continent-wide counterpart to what individual grid operators had already required regionally. It is the point at which ride-through capability stops being a regional differentiator and becomes a baseline everywhere.

The market in which developers sell projects to owners before commercial operation. Prices are quoted per megawatt and rise with development stage; the buyer is usually an IPP or fund that finances and builds.

A corporate credit line that funds development costs before a project reaches notice to proceed — interconnection deposits, permits, land, equipment down-payments. Lenders underwrite the pipeline and the sponsor, not a single contracted project.

Structural elements cast in a factory under controlled conditions and delivered to site to be erected. It moves work off the critical path and out of the weather, at the cost of transport limits and long lead times.

A circuit that charges a unit's capacitors gently through a resistor or a controlled switch before the main connection closes, so a live insertion does not draw a damaging inrush surge. It is the quiet engineering that makes hot-swap possible.
The estimating, planning, constructability review and procurement work done before construction starts. It is where a schedule is either made possible or quietly made impossible.

Capital that sits between debt and ordinary equity: it is paid a fixed return before the owners receive anything, but it has no fixed maturity like a loan. Projects use it to take out construction debt when a long-term loan is not available or wanted.
Paying for capacity before it is delivered. In compute contracts a prepayment funds the supplier's build and shifts delivery risk onto the buyer, who has paid for something that does not yet exist.

The pressure a fluid loses as it flows through pipes, fittings, connectors and cold-plate channels — the head the CDU's pumps must supply at design flow or the far racks starve. Narrow lines multiply it: a 1-inch branch can lose over five times the pressure of a 2-inch one.

How much a gas turbine's compressor raises the pressure of the air passing through it, typically in the high teens to low twenties on a modern heavy-duty machine. Along with firing temperature it sets the cycle's efficiency, and raising it costs compressor stages, which is one reason turbines grow rather than simply improve.

A legally set floor rate for a trade in a locality, applied where public money or certain tax benefits are involved. It removes wage as a competitive variable on those projects, so contractors compete on productivity, supervision and schedule instead.

Scheduled inspection and servicing performed before anything has failed — cooling systems, coolant condition, filters, connections, detection systems, software. The unglamorous items are the ones that matter: skipped coolant and filter service degrades thermal performance silently, and thermal performance is what sets ageing rate.

A data-center valuation shorthand: the price or appraisal of a building divided by its critical IT capacity. It lets a securitization appraisal, a sale and a construction budget be compared on one axis.
A plant split into a constant-flow loop through the chillers and a variable-flow loop out to the load, joined by a short bypass. Simple to control, and it hides a low delta-T rather than exposing it.

The machine that turns fuel into shaft power — a reciprocating engine, a gas turbine or a fuel cell stack driving a generator. Naming it separately matters because the prime mover sets the start time, the load-acceptance behaviour, the emissions profile and the maintenance interval, while the electrical end is comparatively interchangeable.

Generation that carries a site's full load continuously, as its main source — the opposite of standby plant that sits idle until the normal supply fails. The distinction changes the machine, the air permit, and the maintenance regime, so a plant sold as prime and a plant sold as backup are different products even when the hardware looks alike.

An investment a firm makes with its own balance-sheet money rather than with money raised from clients. The firm keeps all the gain and bears all the loss, unlike fund investing where it takes a fee and a slice.
Trading with your own capital and balance sheet, taking the risk and the profit. Contrast with agency trading, where the firm executes a customer's order for a commission and never owns the asset.

A battery cell in a rigid rectangular can, as opposed to a cylinder or a soft pouch. The flat faces pack together with little wasted space and the can carries structural load, which is why grid storage has converged on very large prismatic formats.

A campus electrical system that generates, distributes and manages its own power behind the meter, buying from the public grid only as a supplement or reserve. It replicates generation and distribution; it still depends on the utility for any grid tie and on regulators for permits.

ERCOT's term for a site with its own generation and load behind one point of connection to the grid — an industrial plant or a data-center campus that generates part of what it consumes. Its net position is what the grid sees; the rules on what such a site owes for the grid it leans on are the co-location argument in Texas form.

The largest loss a site is expected to suffer from a defined event under stated assumptions. It sets how much cover is bought and how much capital a carrier holds against the risk, and it is an engineering estimate, not an observed number.
Heat delivered to an industrial plant as steam or hot gas to run chemical, refining or manufacturing processes — a product a reactor or gas plant can sell alongside or instead of electricity.

The generation of manufacturing technology a chip is made on, named by a number in nanometres that is now a marketing label rather than a measurement of anything. A newer node generally means more transistors in the same area and less energy per operation, and access to the newest one is rationed by the foundry.
The laboratory test that establishes the maximum dry density a given soil can reach and the moisture content at which it reaches it. Field compaction is then specified as a percentage of that number.

A certification body's public record that a specific product model has been tested to a standard and is under its surveillance, allowing the manufacturer to apply the body's mark. 'UL 9540 listed' means a laboratory has certified the system to that standard, not that it has been fire-tested at installation scale.

The ratio of planned hours to hours actually earned against installed quantity, tracked weekly. Because it measures work in place rather than time elapsed, it is the earliest honest signal a project gives — a job can look on schedule and be consuming its margin, and this is where that shows first.

Insurance designed for one narrow class of risk and sold as a package — every solar plant, every battery site, every dental practice — usually underwritten by a specialist agency on a carrier's paper. It is how a market gets built for a risk class too new or too small for individual underwriting.

An agreement in which a capital partner commits to fund a series of a developer's projects on pre-agreed terms, rather than negotiating one deal at a time. The commitment figure (USD 3.2 billion, USD 5 billion) is capacity, not money spent.

A contracting model in which the builder is chosen early on qualifications and works with the owner to develop the design, scope and price in stages before a fixed-price construction contract is signed — used for first-of-a-kind plants where the price cannot be known up front.

The current US statutory category that decides whether a company can claim clean-energy tax credits or contribute content to a project that does. It combines a named-entity test with a control test, and it replaced the older foreign-entity-of-concern framing for these credits in 2025.

Bonds issued by a single-purpose company whose only assets are one project — a campus, its substation and its lease — sold to institutional investors instead of borrowed from banks. The credit is the tenant's, the collateral is the campus, and the sponsor's equity is a thin slice beneath the bondholders.

Debt raised by a single project's own entity and repaid only from that project's cash flows, secured on its contracts and assets rather than on the sponsor's balance sheet. Lenders underwrite the contract, the builder and the counterparty, not the parent.

An online platform where developers list projects for sale and buyers bid — LevelTen Energy's is the one Available Power used for Greenport. It turns the pre-COD sale from a private negotiation into an auction.

The performance fee a fund manager earns when a vehicle it manages beats an agreed return. For a landlord that manages third-party money it is real income, but it is lumpy and unrelated to how the buildings performed that quarter.

A rule that makes adding a block to a blockchain expensive on purpose: computers race to find a number that, when hashed with the block's data, produces an output below a target. There is no shortcut — only guessing — so the work is a real cost that an attacker would also have to pay.

A hedge in which a counterparty pays a wind or solar project a fixed amount and receives the project's proxy revenue — a formula of measured resource times price — so that both resource and price risk are swapped away. A parametric wind hedge is the resource-only cousin.

The commission's after-the-fact test of whether a utility's spending was reasonable when the decision was made; imprudent cost is disallowed and falls on shareholders instead of customers. It is the reason a regulated buyer cares so much about a supplier's bankability and paperwork: every purchase must survive this review years later.

Public safety power shutoff: deliberately de-energizing lines in high-risk areas during extreme wind and dry conditions so that a fallen wire cannot start a fire. It trades certain outages for uncertain fires, and a utility is criticized for calling one and sued for not calling one.

A US federal tax credit paid per megawatt-hour generated over a project's first ten years, historically the principal support for wind. Unlike an investment credit, which rewards capital spent, it rewards output, so it favours high-capacity-factor resources. The 2025 budget law ends it for wind and solar placed in service after 2027 where construction begins after July 4, 2026.

The state body that regulates a monopoly utility: it approves rates, certifies new plants and lines, reviews the integrated resource plan and decides what the utility may recover from customers. Called a PUC, a PSC or, in Virginia, the State Corporation Commission — whatever the name, nothing a regulated utility buys at scale is final until it has been through this body.

Power usage effectiveness: total facility power divided by the power that reaches the IT equipment. A PUE of 1.0 would mean every watt went to computing; the gap above it is cooling, conversion, and lighting overhead — the industry's headline efficiency number.

A very short discharge and recovery — hundreds of milliseconds rather than hours. Rack-level backup cells are rated in hundreds of thousands of them, which is a different life metric from the cycle count quoted on a grid battery.

The list of minor incomplete or defective items outstanding at substantial completion, which the contractor must close before final completion. Closing it routinely takes longer than the commissioning that preceded it, because damages have stopped and the crews have gone — the owner's only remaining leverage is the retention it still holds.

How an acquirer's accountants split what it paid among the things it bought — property and equipment, debt taken on, and the remainder called goodwill. It is the one audited statement of what a private company was worth.

The framed, glazed assembly of interconnected solar cells that is the unit of installation on a solar site — typically 2 to 2.5 metres long and 25 to 35 kilograms, which is why placing them is the most labour-intensive step in building a solar plant.

Pulse-width modulation: controlling a converter by switching fully on and fully off at a fixed rate and varying only the fraction of each cycle spent on — the duty cycle. A switch that is either fully on or fully off wastes little, which is the basic reason switching converters beat the old linear ones.

An electrochemical route to separating usable material from spent metallic fuel in molten salt, developed alongside metallic-fuel fast reactors. It recovers fuel without the aqueous chemistry of conventional reprocessing.

The ERCOT-registered entity that submits offers, bids and telemetry for a generator or battery and settles its charges — the trading desk's licence. An owner can be its own QSE or hire one; a 'Level 4' QSE handles the full energy and ancillary-service settlement.

A project's place in line for a grid connection, fixed by the date it applied. Earlier positions get studied first and face fewer upgrade costs, so a good queue position is a tradable asset in its own right.

The coupling at each server hose and manifold port that lets a server be unplugged from a live coolant loop. Dry-break (drip-less) designs close a valve in each half as they separate; blind-mate versions engage as the server slides in. Connections outnumber pipes, so they are the dominant leak risk and are colour-coded and leak-tested.

A proportional reinsurance structure: the reinsurer takes a fixed percentage of every premium and pays the same percentage of every loss. Simple, capital-efficient for the cedent, and indifferent to how large any one loss is.

A resource-adequacy contract: a California load-serving entity pays a battery a fixed monthly amount per megawatt for being available to meet the buyer's capacity obligation, whoever dispatches it. The contract is the reason most CAISO batteries get financed.

Assembling, cabling, cooling, powering and testing a complete rack in a factory so it arrives at the site ready to switch on, rather than shipping loose servers to be built up on the floor. The industry labels the depth of this work — roughly, components, then a built server, then a fully integrated and tested rack — and how far up that ladder a vendor goes is a large part of what distinguishes rack vendors from each other.

The vertical supply and return pipes in a rack that split the row's coolant to each server's hoses through quick disconnects and collect it again — stainless steel, built for the rack standard (EIA, ORV3, MGX) and height, leak-tested before shipment, and the place where flow to each server is set.

The standard height increment of equipment mounted in a rack, written as U — one unit is 1.75 inches, and a full-height rack is normally 42 to 52 of them. Every server and power shelf is described by how many it occupies, so U is the currency in which rack space is spent.

The years a large-load tariff gives a new customer to grow into its contracted demand before the minimum bill applies in full — a schedule such as forty percent in year one, sixty in year two, then the whole contract demand. It recognizes that a campus energizes in halls, and it is the term a developer negotiates hardest after the term itself.
The temperature drop a cooling tower actually produces between the water entering it and the water leaving. Range times flow is the heat the tower is rejecting.

The steam cycle: boil water, expand the steam through a turbine, condense it, pump it back. In a combined-cycle plant it is the bottoming half, run entirely on heat the gas turbine would otherwise have vented — which is why the second turbine adds output without adding fuel.

The value of a regulated utility's plant in service — generation, wires, substations, meters — net of depreciation, on which the commission lets it earn a return. Every dollar of prudently built plant that goes into rate base earns the allowed return for decades, which is why a regulated utility's growth story is a capital-spending story and why it would rather own an asset than contract for one.

The commission proceeding in which a utility's base rates are reset: the utility files its costs and rate base, intervenors test them, and an order sets the revenue requirement, the allowed return and the rate classes for the years ahead. Virginia runs Dominion Energy Virginia's as a biennial review. It is the moment a large-load tariff can be created or rewritten.

A group of customers billed under the same tariff schedule — residential, small commercial, large industrial, and now very large loads — because they cost the utility different amounts to serve. Creating a rate class is how a commission fences a data center's costs off from everyone else's bill.

An agreement or order holding a utility's base rates flat for a set period, usually in exchange for something — a settled case, deferred costs, a political truce before an election. Costs still accrue; the freeze decides when customers pay them, not whether.

Premium divided by the limit of cover bought, expressed as a percentage — pay 10 million for 100 million of cover and the rate on line is 10%. It is the standard way to compare the price of catastrophe cover between layers, years and markets.

A voluntary commitment, launched in 2026, under which a data-center developer promises to bring or pay for its own power supply and delivery infrastructure, pay for capacity whether used or not, and invest locally. It does not itself change how a utility allocates costs.

A firm (S&P, Moody's, Fitch, Morningstar DBRS, KBRA) that grades a bond's likelihood of paying. The grade sets the coupon; agencies disagree about whether single-tenant data centers can be top-rated collateral.

The contractual date on which a data-center building is complete, commissioned and available for the tenant to move in — the day rent starts. Delay damages and the landlord's construction-loan interest both hang on it.

A project with land, permits, interconnection and (where needed) offtake all in hand, lacking only money and a contractor. It is the most valuable point for a developer to sell, because the buyer takes construction risk and little else.

ERCOT's December 2025 redesign in which energy and ancillary services are cleared together every five minutes rather than ancillary services being procured a day ahead. A battery's state of charge is tracked in the clearing, which changes how a one-hour unit is paid.

The wholesale market that settles actual delivery in short intervals, typically five minutes, correcting the differences between what was committed the day before and what the grid actually needs. Its prices are far more volatile than day-ahead prices, which is where most of a merchant battery's upside and risk sits.
The moment a fund sells an investment and turns a paper gain into cash. Managers' earnings are lumpy because realisations are lumpy — a single large sale can dominate a quarter.

A liquid-cooled radiator that replaces a rack's back door and neutralises the servers' hot exhaust air before it reaches the room, while the servers themselves stay air-cooled. The transitional step that brings liquid to the rack without touching the IT hardware.

Changing who funds a company and on what terms — new common or preferred equity, new debt, a refinancing — usually to fund growth or replace maturing capital without necessarily changing who runs it. Prime Data Centers has been recapitalised five times while remaining founder-controlled.

The sequence of forms a founder-owned developer raises money in without giving up control: a strategic partner, institutional co-investors, a joint-control arrangement, a joint-venture cheque, preferred equity at the parent, then project-level debt building by building. Each rung has a price in consent rights or coupon.

An engine that burns fuel inside cylinders to push pistons and turn a crankshaft, which spins a generator. Built in units of a few megawatts and stacked into hundreds, it delivers fast, keeps its efficiency at part load, and gives a plant real spinning mass — at the cost of many machines to maintain and a large site footprint.

A side contract between a landlord, its tenant and a third party in which the third party promises that, if the tenant defaults or goes bankrupt, it will either pay the rent and step into the lease or pay a termination fee. It is how a guarantor's credit is attached to someone else's lease.

A workplace injury or illness serious enough to be counted under the regulator's definition — beyond first aid, involving medical treatment, restricted duty, lost time or a diagnosed condition. Because the definition is regulatory rather than discretionary, it is what makes safety records comparable between firms at all.
A power-electronics device that turns AC into DC — the first stage of nearly every power supply, charger, and data-center power shelf.

A cap on how much money investors can withdraw from a fund in one period, usually a percentage of net asset value per quarter. When requests exceed the cap everyone is paid a proportional share, which is called prorating.

Moving a company's legal home from one country to another. It changes which regulator it reports to, which rules govern shareholders, and often which exchange it lists on — so filings from before and after the move are not directly comparable.

The working fluid in a cooling circuit, which absorbs heat where it evaporates and releases it where it condenses. Which one a product uses is increasingly a regulatory matter as well as an engineering one, since refrigerants differ widely in flammability and in their effect on the atmosphere.

A cost a utility has incurred but not yet recovered, which the commission has agreed may be collected from customers in the future. It sits on the balance sheet as an asset because a regulator's promise of recovery has value. Deferring costs into a regulatory asset lets a utility spend ahead of a rate case, at the price of a later prudence review that can disallow the deferral.

Assets under management as defined by the SEC for Form ADV — the gross value of the portfolios an adviser manages with discretion; it can differ from the 'equity capital' or 'AUM' a firm quotes in press releases.

The gap between when a utility spends money and when a rate order lets it recover that money. Long lag erodes the earned return below the allowed one; riders, formula rate plans and CWIP recovery all exist to shorten it.

A term that restores a catastrophe layer's limit after a loss has used it, usually for an extra premium and usually a limited number of times. Whether a layer has one, several or none is a material difference in a season with two events.

Insurance bought by insurers: a reinsurer takes a share of a carrier's risk in exchange for a share of its premium, spreading catastrophe exposure across the global market. Named reinsurers behind a programme are a signal of its capacity and its credit quality.

A broker whose client is an insurance company rather than a policyholder. It designs and places the treaties and facultative cover that let a carrier write more risk than its own capital would allow, and it advises on how much risk to keep. The work is capital structuring dressed as broking.

A real estate investment trust: a company that earns mostly rent-like income and distributes at least 90% of its taxable income to shareholders, and in exchange pays no corporate income tax. Data centres qualify because renting space, power and cooling counts as property income.

An agreement that keeps a plant its owner wants to retire running because the grid operator has found the system cannot yet do without it. The owner is paid its costs under a regulated rate, and the region's customers pay, until transmission or new generation removes the need.

PJM's forward capacity auction, which procures the capability the region will need several years ahead and sets a single clearing price for it. Winning a commitment turns a project's future availability into contracted revenue before it is built.

The engineer's written agreement that a named party other than its client — a new lender, a buyer of the project — may rely on its report, usually under the same liability cap. Without one, a report found in a data room is information, not something the reader can sue over.

A distribution cabinet placed out on the data-hall floor, fed from a larger upstream board, that breaks power out into the branch circuits serving racks. It shortens the runs to the load and puts metering and breakers where the equipment actually is.

A tradable certificate representing the environmental attributes of one megawatt-hour of renewable generation, separable from the electricity itself. Buying certificates alone matches consumption on paper; buying them bundled with the power from a named new plant is what makes a purchase additional.
A clause raising rent by a fixed percentage each year (2–3% is common in data-center leases). Over a 15–20-year term it compounds into a large share of the contract's headline value.
What it would cost today to build the same asset from scratch, including land, power and equipment. It is a floor under the value of an existing building when new supply is slow or constrained.

Replacing the turbines, and often the foundations, on an existing wind site while keeping its land rights and grid connection. A repower typically raises output substantially on the same acreage and restarts the asset's depreciation and warranty life, because the valuable part of an old wind farm is its interconnection, not its hardware.

A supply framework in which a buyer reserves manufacturing capacity or volume (in GWh or units) for future projects, with prices and slots fixed but individual purchase orders drawn down later as projects are ready.
Capacity a tenant holds an option or right of first refusal on, with no rent commitment yet. Counted above contracted capacity in a landlord's pipeline; worth a schedule, not a cash flow.

A promise, usually by the chip maker or designer, to cover part of the value of leased hardware at the end of the lease. It removes the lessor's biggest fear — that the chips will be worth nothing — and is what makes multi-billion chip leases financeable.
ERCOT's main contingency reserve: capacity held ready to respond within seconds to a plant tripping offline. Batteries can sell it, and for several years it paid more than energy arbitrage did.

The insurance broker that holds the relationship with the buyer. It takes the client's risk to market, negotiates terms, places the cover and advocates on claims, and is paid by commission out of the premium or by a fee from the client. It is an agent of the buyer, not of the insurer — which is what separates it from an agent.

A restructured market in which the wires company delivers power but customers buy the energy from competing retailers, and generation is not in rate base. Most of Texas works this way inside ERCOT; the Southeast and MISO South do not, which is why a data center there signs with one integrated utility rather than a retailer and a wires company.

A percentage withheld from every progress payment until the work is finished, released at final completion. It gives the contractor a reason to return and finish the unglamorous end of a job and gives the owner a fund to complete the work if it does not — and because it is usually a large share of the project's whole profit, held without interest for years, it is a financing instrument rather than an accounting detail.

Reinsurance bought by reinsurers. It is the last layer of the chain that moves a catastrophe loss off any single balance sheet, and when retro capacity tightens the effect works back down through reinsurance to the price of a project's property policy.

A contract in which a counterparty guarantees a merchant project a minimum annual revenue in exchange for a fee, leaving the upside with the owner. It is the instrument that lets a battery with no offtaker borrow, because the lender can size debt to the floor.

The total a utility is allowed to collect from customers over a period: operating costs plus depreciation plus taxes plus the allowed return on rate base. A rate case is an argument about this one number, and the tariffs are how it is divided among customer classes.

The set of separate payments one asset earns at the same time — energy arbitrage, ancillary services, capacity payments, contracted fees — which together decide whether it is viable. The same battery in two different markets can have completely different stacks, and comparing projects on any single layer is misleading.

A financial contract in which a battery owner exchanges its uncertain market revenue for fixed payments from a counterparty — the counterparty takes the price risk and the owner gets bankable cash flow. GridStor's April 2026 agreement with Axpo on Hidden Lakes is one.
Forcing water through a membrane at pressure so that dissolved salts are left behind. It produces very pure water and a concentrated reject stream that has to go somewhere.

The brief backwards current a diode draws while it stops conducting, because stored charge has to be swept out first. That current flows through the opposite switch at full bus voltage, so it appears as heat and as a spike of electrical noise.

A bank line a company can draw, repay and redraw up to a limit — working-capital liquidity rather than project debt. A large syndicated revolver is a sign banks treat the company as an established borrower.

Request for proposals: the competitive solicitation a utility issues for the capacity its plan calls for — a storage-specific, solar or all-source RFP — evaluated by the utility or an independent evaluator and then taken to the commission for approval. For an equipment vendor it is the moment the bidding developer's bill of materials locks, which is earlier than the award.

The US federal air-toxics rule for stationary reciprocating internal combustion engines, which sets what an engine may emit and how many hours a year an emergency unit may run outside a genuine outage — commonly 100 hours for maintenance and testing, of which only a limited share may be non-emergency demand response. It is the rule that decides whether a backup fleet can be monetised.

Staying connected and operating through a grid disturbance — a voltage dip or a frequency excursion — instead of protectively disconnecting. Grid codes increasingly require it of both resources and very large loads, for a blunt reason: if everything connected trips at the first sign of trouble, a local fault becomes a system-wide one.

A separate line on the bill that recovers one program's cost outside the base rates — a new plant, a transmission program, offshore wind, fuel. Riders let a utility start earning on a project without waiting for the next rate case, which is why regulators guard them and why a utility's biggest projects each tend to arrive with one.

A tenant's contractual right to be offered a landlord's next building or adjacent land before anyone else (first offer) or to match a third party's terms (first refusal). How a hyperscaler locks a campus without leasing all of it.

The small alternating current superimposed on a battery's direct current by the charger or the inverter. It heats the cell from the inside and ages it, which is why the acceptable level is a published specification rather than an afterthought.

Money set aside to absorb losses rather than to earn a return — an insurer's surplus, a captive's reserves, a cat bond's collateral, a developer's contingency. Framing insurance as risk capital makes visible that every policy is somebody's balance sheet rented for a year.

The share of a loss a business decides to carry itself, through deductibles, self-insured layers or a captive, rather than transfer to an insurer. Raising it is the cheapest way to cut premium and the fastest way to turn a bad year into a very bad one.

Renewable natural gas: biogas from a landfill, digester or wastewater plant that has been cleaned and upgraded until it meets pipeline specification. Raw biogas is heavily diluted with carbon dioxide and often carries sulphur and moisture, so it needs far greater volume for the same heat and will poison catalysts if burned untreated.

AMD's open software platform for running computation on its GPUs — its answer to CUDA. Whether a given model, framework or library runs well on it is the practical question that decides how substitutable AMD silicon is for NVIDIA's.

Rate of change of frequency: how fast grid frequency falls in the seconds after generation is suddenly lost. A grid with plenty of spinning mass falls slowly; one dominated by inverters falls fast enough that protection settings written for the old world mis-trip in the new one.

Investigating a failure until the mechanism is identified rather than the occasion — not that a batch was bad, but which parameter drifted and why the control did not catch it. The test of whether an organisation really does it is whether its corrective actions ever change a design or a control system rather than only adding an inspection.

A UPS built around a rotating synchronous machine rather than power electronics: the machine, fed through a choke, generates a clean sine wave for the load, and a flywheel on its shaft supplies the energy when the input fails. It has no battery, delivers a large fault current, isolates the load from harmonics on the supply and connects readily at medium voltage; its costs are bearings, maintenance and a few points of efficiency.

The share of energy put into a storage system that comes back out after conversion and thermal losses — typically in the high-80s percent range for lithium-ion. The gap is energy bought but never sold.

PJM's Regional Transmission Expansion Plan: the annual process in which the grid operator identifies reliability needs, opens competitive windows and assigns transmission projects — with their cost allocation — to utilities and developers. The billion-dollar lines into a data-center cluster are chosen here, years before they are built.

Regional transmission organization: the FERC-regulated operator that runs the wholesale markets, the interconnection queue and the regional transmission plan across many utilities — PJM, MISO, SPP. A regulated utility inside one still owns its wires and plants, but the price of capacity and the plan for the big lines are set at the RTO, one level above its own commission.

The US rule that lets securities be sold quickly to large institutional investors without SEC registration. Most data-center project bonds are 144A (and Reg S offshore) offerings, which is why their terms surface through bond marketing and press reports rather than public filings.

The latest month's (or week's) revenue multiplied out to a year — a snapshot of current pace, not an audited annual figure. Companies disclose it at funding events; it can move faster than any fiscal year shows.

Starting a project far enough — by spending, or by taking delivery of equipment — to lock in the tax rules in force at that moment, even if those rules later change. It creates a cohort of owners still buying under older terms, and therefore a procurement channel whose constraints differ from everyone else's.

A formal auction in which an owner, through investment banks it has mandated, invites bids for a company or platform. 'Exploring strategic alternatives' is the polite first stage; naming the banks is the public one.
A state incentive that removes sales or use tax on the servers and equipment a data center buys, which can be the largest recurring tax on a campus. Several states paused or capped these in 2026.

A lease so long or so complete that accounting treats it as effectively selling the asset to the tenant: the landlord books a receivable and much of the profit up front instead of rent over time. Whether a data-centre lease qualifies changes the reported earnings profile enormously.
A comparison limited to properties owned throughout both periods being compared, so growth is not flattered by acquisitions or new construction. Landlords often call it same-capital.

The 2025 Texas law setting the terms on which very large loads connect to the grid: screening-study fees and proof of site control up front, mandatory curtailment protocols, and disclosure of on-site backup generation. It is the template other states are copying, and it is what makes a data center's ability to shed or buffer load a condition of connecting at all.

Supervisory control and data acquisition: the operator's window onto a plant — live telemetry out, remote commands in. It is a visibility and intervention layer rather than a deciding one; the automated control loops below it are acting far faster than anyone is watching.

The two ways AI machines are wired together. Scale-up is the memory-speed link that makes a group of GPUs behave as one accelerator — it rides copper, so its reach is about one rack. Scale-out is the switched network between racks, with longer latency and protocol overhead, which is why so much engineering effort goes into packing more compute and more power into that single rack-sized domain.

Virginia's State Corporation Commission — the state's public utility commission, a three-judge body that sets Dominion Energy Virginia's rates in biennial reviews, certifies its plants and lines, reviews its integrated resource plan and approved its large-load rate class. Its dockets are the primary record of how Data Center Alley gets its power.

Recovering time by adding hours or crews rather than by moving the completion date. Its cost is not linear in the time recovered: sustained overtime returns less per hour as weeks accumulate and extra crews in a fixed area interfere with each other, so the productivity lost is real, expensive and very hard to evidence afterwards.
A compressor in which two meshing helical rotors trap gas and squeeze it as it moves along them. Tolerant of high lift and of part load, and physically smaller than a centrifugal for the same duty.
A compressor formed by two interleaved spirals, one orbiting inside the other, sweeping gas inward. Simple, quiet, and the standard building block of small and modular machines.

The closed loop of clean coolant that runs between a distribution unit and the cold plates in the racks, kept separate from the building's own chilled-water loop. Separating them lets the rack loop be filtered, treated and pressure-controlled independently of the facility.

A sale of existing shares by current holders — often employees or early investors — to a new buyer, so the company itself receives no new money; contrast a primary round, which issues new shares for cash.

A US Department of Defense list of companies identified as Chinese military companies operating in the United States. Appearing on it triggers defence contracting restrictions, and it is a separate list from the battery-specific procurement ban — a company can be on one and not the other.
US tariffs on Chinese imports imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act — including steep rates on lithium-ion batteries — that reshape the landed cost of China-sourced storage hardware.

The U.S. trade statute under which the International Trade Commission investigates imported products accused of infringing a U.S. patent. Its remedy is not damages but an exclusion order — the product is stopped at the border — which makes it a fast and heavy lever in hardware patent disputes.

Financing a specific approved cost — storm damage, a retired plant — by selling bonds backed by a dedicated charge on customer bills, so the utility recovers the money at once at a low interest rate instead of carrying it in rate base for years. Common after Gulf hurricanes.

The Southeast Energy Exchange Market — a bilateral, fifteen-minute trading platform among Southeastern utilities that are not in any RTO. It is not a market operator: there is no central dispatch, no capacity auction and no queue; each utility remains its own balancing authority.

How a listed group reports results by business line rather than by subsidiary. A private landlord inside a 'data' segment is visible only as a share of the segment's cash flow, mixed with its siblings.

Demonstrating that equipment and its mountings survive the ground motion a site's code requires. It is a design case rather than a formality — it drives internal bracing and anchor design — and because requirements vary by jurisdiction, the same product can be compliant on one side of a boundary and not the other.

Exhaust after-treatment that injects a urea or ammonia solution across a catalyst to convert nitrogen oxides into nitrogen and water. It is the standard control that lets a diesel or gas plant meet a tight air permit, and it is equipment, space and a consumable rather than a setting.

Arranging breakers in series so a fault trips only the nearest device upstream of it, cutting the failure away surgically while the rest of the building keeps running. Engineers nest the devices' time-current curves so the downstream breaker always wins the race; without it, a rack-level fault can open a main breaker and darken a whole hall.

A utility's proposal to build and own a plant itself, evaluated against third-party bids in an all-source solicitation. Because owned plant enters rate base and a contract does not, commissions watch whether the self-build was compared fairly with the bids.

Operating mining machines you own, for your own account, and keeping the bitcoin. Contrast with hosting, where you sell power, space and operations to someone else who owns the machines and takes the price risk.
Work a general contractor executes with its own directly employed craft workforce rather than subcontracting it. It buys schedule control and cost visibility on the scopes that drive the programme.

Safety extra-low voltage: a supply below about 60 volts DC that the safety standards treat as safe to touch, so it can be handled, wired and serviced without the insulation, clearances and lockout that higher voltages demand. The 48-volt rack bus sits deliberately just under that line.

A cell whose electrolyte is a gel or a hybrid of solid and liquid rather than a free liquid. It is a step toward solid-state rather than the arrival of it — and vendors' 'solid-state' branding frequently means exactly this, which is worth checking.

Bonds that rank first among a borrower's debts and carry a lien on named assets — the campus and the equity of its holding company in Fleet's Storey County deals. 'Senior' is the queue position in a default; 'secured' is what the holders can take.

The share of a cooling load that lowers air temperature rather than condensing moisture out of it. IT heat is almost entirely sensible, which is why equipment for data halls is built differently from comfort air conditioning.

The written control logic for how a building's plant stages, ramps and recovers — which machine starts when, to what setpoint, and in what order after an event. Two identical plants with different sequences differ enormously in energy use and in how they behave during an outage; it is the most consequential invisible thing in a facility.

How many cells are wired in series and how many of those strings sit in parallel, usually written as a pair of numbers. The series count is set by the direct-current bus voltage the conversion equipment expects; the parallel count is set by how much energy the enclosure is meant to hold.

The part of a service contract defining how quickly a supplier must respond to and resolve faults, graded by severity. What matters is the definition of severity and when the clock starts — a response measured from a ticket the owner must raise behaves very differently from one triggered by remote monitoring.

A minimum distance a local ordinance requires between energy equipment and a property line, home or road. Setbacks decide how much of a leased site is actually usable, and a rule change can shrink a viable project below the size that justified the land.

A negotiated resolution of a regulatory proceeding, signed by the utility and some or all intervening parties and submitted to the commission for approval. A settlement can be unopposed, meaning every party signed, or contested. Commissions are not bound by settlements and can modify or reject them, which is the difference between agreeing with your opponents and winning.

The node or hub at which a resource is paid ERCOT's locational price. Two batteries a few miles apart can earn different prices when a transmission constraint binds between them — which is why owners talk about 'nodes', not a single Texas price.

A thunderstorm complex producing large hail, straight-line wind or tornadoes — the peril class that has driven the largest share of insured losses in the United States since 2020 and the one that prices utility-scale solar. Named windstorms (hurricanes) are treated as a separate peril.

Sulphur hexafluoride: an exceptionally good electrical insulator and arc quencher, and one of the most potent greenhouse gases known. That combination is why it is used at all and why its leak rate is regulated.

Switchgear that replaces sulphur hexafluoride with dried natural-origin air or a lower-warming fluorinated gas, usually paired with vacuum interruption because clean air is a much poorer arc quencher on its own.
The one-way hashing function bitcoin mining uses. It turns any input into a fixed 256-bit output that cannot be run backwards, so the only way to hit a target output is to try inputs until one works.

Building the enclosure, structure and base services of a facility while leaving the interior fit-out for a later scope or a different contractor. It is how a data hall gets built ahead of knowing exactly what will go in it.

The fault in which both switches of a half-bridge conduct at once, putting the full supply across two devices in series with almost nothing to limit the current. It is usually fatal to the devices and is what dead time exists to prevent.

The calculation of how much current would flow at every point in an electrical system if it faulted there, given every source that can contribute — the utility, the generators, and the motors that briefly act as generators as they spin down. It sets the interrupting rating every breaker must meet and is the input both the coordination study and the arc-flash calculation run on.

A buyer's own bottom-up estimate of what a product ought to cost to build, assembled from materials, labour, overhead and a fair margin. It exists so the buyer can negotiate against an analysis rather than against a quote.

Silicon carbide: a wide-bandgap semiconductor that switches faster with lower losses than silicon, at higher voltages and temperatures — the material behind smaller, more efficient inverters and converters.

A conversion cabinet standing beside a rack that produces the rack's high-voltage DC bus from whatever the building already distributes. It is a bridge product by design: it delivers a new power architecture to one rack without rebuilding the hall around it — which is also the precise boundary of what it fixes, since the hall's upstream capacity is unchanged.

A gas turbine that drives a generator and vents its hot exhaust rather than recovering it. Cheaper, faster to build, and quick to start, but only roughly 35 to 40 percent of the fuel's energy reaches the wires — which is why it survives as a peaking and bridge machine rather than as baseload.

A fixed-ratio converter that drives its transformer with a pure sine-wave current at resonance and switches its transistors only as that current passes through zero, so almost nothing is wasted in the switching itself. The idea lets a current multiplier run at very high frequency, which shrinks its magnetics and raises its density.

The steel structure that rotates a row of solar modules east to west through the day, following the sun on one axis. Trackers raise annual energy yield by roughly 15-25% over fixed-tilt mounting and are the standard for utility-scale solar, but they add moving parts, torque tubes and motors that construction crews must install and align precisely.

A turbine blade cast as one continuous metal crystal, with no grain boundaries for creep to open up. Grain boundaries are where hot metal under load slowly pulls apart, so removing them buys perhaps another fifty degrees of firing temperature — and each blade is a slow, expensive casting.

The one-page electrical drawing that shows a facility's power path — utility service, transformers, switchgear, transfer switches, UPS and distribution — as single lines rather than individual conductors. It is the document a power-room conversation actually happens over, because every redundancy claim is visible on it.
A campus or building leased entirely to one customer, typically a hyperscaler. Simplest to build and finance, and the most concentrated: one tenant's decision empties the whole asset.
Testing the installed equipment on site, energised and in its final configuration, before the owner accepts it. It proves the installation, where the works test proved the machine.

Having the legal right to build on a parcel — an option, a lease or ownership — before spending on studies and permits. Without it a project is a drawing; with it the interconnection request can be filed.

A long-term lease of a parcel from a landowner on which a developer builds a battery, paying rent instead of buying the land. Available Power's model leased commercial land from real-estate owners for small batteries.

A concrete floor cast directly on prepared ground rather than spanning between supports. It is the working surface of a data hall, and its flatness and load rating are specifications, not by-products.

A pipe cast through a concrete wall or slab so that conduit, piping or busway can pass through it later without cutting structure. Sleeves are set from coordinated drawings before the pour, not afterwards.

The document that records the terms of a placement and the shares each underwriter has taken, signed line by line down the market. A subscription market places one risk across many insurers this way rather than asking one to take it whole.

A payment that holds a place in a manufacturer's production schedule before the equipment has been specified, sometimes before it has been designed. In a shortage it is the queue position, not the price, that is being bought.

Small modular reactor: a nuclear plant designed as factory-built units of roughly 50 to 300 MW each rather than one gigawatt-class build, meant to be licensed once and repeated. None is yet operating commercially in the United States; for a utility and a hyperscaler the attraction is clean, dispatchable power on an existing nuclear site, and the constraint is a licensing and construction clock measured in a decade.

A fast reactor cooled by liquid sodium, which boils near 880 C and so runs at essentially atmospheric pressure. That removes the thick pressure vessel, and adds a metal that burns on contact with air or water.
A battery chemistry replacing lithium with abundant sodium — cheaper materials and better cold-weather performance at lower energy density; an emerging challenger for stationary storage.

The opposite of a hard market: capacity exceeds demand, prices fall, terms broaden and underwriters compete on more than price. It squeezes commission income and it quietly erodes the value of anything sold as a way to earn a discount.

Switching a converter's transistors at the instant the voltage or current across them is zero, so the transition itself dissipates almost nothing. Hard switching — turning off while current still flows — wastes energy on every edge, which limits how fast a converter can switch and therefore how small it can be.

How strongly the ground resists electrical current, measured before design and expressed per unit length. It sets the design of the grounding system and the corrosion allowance on anything buried — two twenty-year decisions taken from a survey done in the first weeks of a project.

Dirt, dust, pollen, salt or bird droppings accumulating on solar modules and blocking light. It builds gradually, is reversed by rain or washing, and is one of the loss mechanisms a monitoring platform is expected to distinguish from an equipment fault.

A solar plant paired with storage large enough that the combined plant can deliver firm output during the evening peak, after the sun has gone. It is sold as a substitute for a gas peaking plant rather than as intermittent generation.

A solar plant and a battery sharing one site and one grid connection, so midday solar can be shifted into the evening. The pairing raises the value of both and lets one interconnection serve two assets.

A fuel cell with a ceramic electrolyte that works only when very hot, roughly 700 to 1,000 degrees Celsius. The heat is the point: at that temperature natural gas breaks down into hydrogen right at the electrode, so the cell runs on pipeline gas rather than purified hydrogen. There is no flame, so nitrogen oxides and particulates are near zero — but the ceramics dislike being cycled and prefer steady output.

A battery that replaces the liquid electrolyte with a solid one, removing the most flammable component and allowing higher-energy electrode pairings. The engineering difficulty is maintaining physical contact between solid layers as they expand and contract with every cycle.

The capital a regulator and the rating agencies require an insurer to hold against the risks it has written. It is the real constraint on how much cover exists in a market — capacity is not appetite, it is somebody's balance-sheet capital priced and allocated.

The rated noise a machine emits, quoted at a stated distance. On a storage or generation site it is frequently a permitting condition rather than a comfort item, and equipment that is compliant only at part-load cooling is not compliant on the hottest afternoon of the year.
The quantity and kind of radioactive material a given accident could release. Almost every downstream siting, staffing and emergency-planning requirement is sized from it.

AI computing capacity located in, and legally controlled from, a particular country so that its data and workloads stay under that country's law. Governments buy it for public services, defence and regulated industries; vendors sell the same racks with a jurisdiction attached.

A state-owned investment fund that invests a government's surplus — oil revenue, reserves or budget surpluses — in companies, property and infrastructure at home and abroad, answering to the state rather than to outside investors.

Starting combustion with an electrical spark at a chosen instant, as almost all large stationary gas engines do. Its counterpart, compression ignition, relies on the heat of compression alone to ignite the charge — which is what a diesel does, and what makes its timing a property of the fuel rather than of the controls.

The gap between what a megawatt-hour of electricity sells for and what the gas to make it costs at a stated efficiency. It is the gross margin of a gas plant, and a merchant gas fleet's earnings are essentially the spark spread multiplied by the hours it is economic to run.

Independent third-party inspection and testing of specific structural work — welds, bolts, concrete, soils — required by code and scheduled in advance. Work covered up before its inspection gets uncovered.
How much power a cell delivers per kilogram of itself, in watts per kilogram. It is the figure of merit for a backup cell, where energy per litre is the figure of merit for a grid cell.

The first half of the US prohibited-foreign-entity test. A company qualifies either by being named on one of several government lists or, more broadly, by being incorporated in or controlled from a covered nation — so incorporation alone can be enough.

How soon a site can actually be energised at the megawatts a customer needs — the constraint that has replaced land and construction cost as the binding one for large loads. A site with an existing grid connection can be worth far more than a better site that must wait years in the queue.
The water-filled bay where discharged fuel sits while its decay heat falls, before it can be moved into dry storage casks. The water is a coolant and a shield at the same time.

Generating units already running and synchronized but deliberately loaded below their capability, so their headroom is available in seconds rather than in the minutes a cold start would take. On an islanded campus it is the margin that absorbs a load swing or a unit trip without the frequency wandering.

A developer built from scratch by a fund that hired the team and supplied the capital, rather than a founder-led company the fund later invested in. GridStor is one: Goldman Sachs assembled it around a project it had already bought.

Southwest Power Pool: the regional grid operator for the central US plains — Oklahoma, Kansas, the Texas Panhandle, Arkansas, Louisiana, the Dakotas and neighbours. Like PJM and MISO it runs the wholesale market, the interconnection queue and a regional transmission plan; it has a capacity requirement on its utilities rather than a centralized capacity auction.
An isolated concrete pad under a column that spreads its load over enough ground to stay within the bearing capacity. The default foundation where the soil is good.

Solid-state circuit breaker: a breaker that interrupts electronically in a fraction of a millisecond, before fault current reaches its peak, instead of physically parting contacts. It is the enabling protection device for DC distribution, where there is no AC zero crossing to help extinguish the arc.

Solid-state transformer: a power-electronics replacement for the iron transformer that converts medium-voltage AC directly to regulated DC using high-frequency switching — a candidate to collapse today's multi-stage data-center power chain into one device.

A building that is complete, energised and leased with the tenant paying rent — the state in which a construction loan can be refinanced by a mortgage or an ABS, and in which a buyer can price it on the rent alone.

A digital asset designed to hold a fixed value, usually one US dollar, by holding reserves against every unit issued. The issuer earns interest on those reserves, which makes it a deposit-like business rather than a speculative one.

A cell built by stacking cut sheets of electrode and separator in layers rather than winding a continuous roll. Very large cell formats increasingly use it because a stack fills a rectangular can more evenly, but it is a different manufacturing process with its own defect population.

Locking up a proof-of-stake blockchain's tokens to help validate its transactions, in return for a share of newly issued tokens. A service provider can do this on customers' behalf and take a cut, which is fee revenue rather than a directional bet.

A field test in which a standard sampler is driven into the soil by a standard hammer and the blows per increment are counted. The blow count is a rough, universally understood index of how dense or stiff the ground is.

A body accredited to write standards through a balanced consensus process — CSA Group, UL Standards & Engagement, NFPA, IEC, ISO. It is distinct from the laboratory that tests to the standard and from the government that adopts it, though one organisation can hold more than one role.

The generator rating for carrying a varying load only while the normal supply is out, for a limited number of hours a year and with no overload allowance. It is the highest kilowatt number the same engine will carry — and the one a data center's backup fleet is bought against, which is why a standby set cannot simply be re-labelled prime.

What a utility charges a customer that makes its own power for standing ready to serve it when that plant is down. The utility must hold capacity for a customer who normally does not draw it, and prices that readiness whether or not it is called on — which is often the largest surprise in a self-generation business case.
The USD 500 billion AI-infrastructure programme announced in January 2025 by OpenAI, SoftBank, Oracle and MGX to build data-centre campuses for OpenAI, starting in Abilene, Texas.

A power-electronic device that injects or absorbs reactive power within milliseconds to hold voltage steady. Far faster than switched capacitors, and it supplies no inertia and almost no fault current of its own.

The fuel gauge: how much energy is on board right now, as a percentage of what the plant can hold. Operators run a narrower window than the physical one because cells age faster held near either extreme, and every dispatch decision is planned around this number.

The long-term gauge: how much capacity a battery still holds compared with when it was new. Where state of charge moves through the day, state of health only ever falls — and how fast it falls is what a capacity warranty is a promise about.

The path around a UPS's conversion stages that connects the load straight to the raw supply — automatically, through a solid-state static switch, when the UPS overloads or fails, or manually, through a maintenance bypass, so the unit can be serviced. While the load is on bypass it is unprotected: the stored seconds are not available.
A solid-state switch that picks between two independent supplies in a few milliseconds, so a load with only one cord can still be fed from both an A and a B path.

A UPS built from power electronics — a rectifier, a DC link with batteries on it and an inverter — with no moving parts except fans. It is the incumbent form in data centers: modular, efficient, factory-built at low voltage, and dependent on a battery room whose chemistry, life and fire code are a design in themselves.

The electricity a power plant itself consumes to run pumps, fans, controls and cooling. It matters in co-location arguments because rules about who may take power from behind a generator's connection were written with station power, not a gigawatt data centre, in mind.

Controlling quality by measuring the parameters of a manufacturing process and watching their distribution, rather than by inspecting the output. It catches a drift before much has been made, which is earlier and far cheaper — but it is blind to any failure mode nobody thought to instrument.

Holding rainwater on site and releasing it slowly so that covering acres in roof and pavement does not flood everything downstream. It is a permit condition, and it occupies land that cannot then be built on.
Capacity that has been paid for but cannot be used because power, cooling, space and redundancy do not line up — a row with spare amps and no cooling takes no more racks.

Investment a utility made to serve a customer or a market that then went away, leaving the plant unpaid for. The fear behind every large-load tariff term — minimum demand, long contracts, collateral, exit fees — is a substation and a gas plant built for a data center that never fully arrives, with the bill landing on everyone else.

An investor that takes a stake and a role — capital plus consultation, co-investment or consent rights — rather than a passive holding. Macquarie Capital's 2021 partnership with Prime paired equity with a ten-year capital plan.

A legal standard under which a party is liable for harm regardless of fault or negligence. In utility wildfire law it means a utility whose equipment ignited a fire pays even if it maintained the line reasonably. Some states apply it or the related doctrine of inverse condemnation; others require proof of negligence. Which standard a state uses is the single largest variable in a utility's wildfire exposure.

Power conversion split into many small units, each serving one group of battery strings, rather than concentrated in one large central converter. Distributing it lets the conversion sit inside the battery enclosure, shrinks the fault current any one unit can contribute, and means a converter failure costs a fraction of the block rather than all of it.
How many degrees below its condensing temperature the liquid refrigerant is when it leaves the condenser. More subcooling means more useful cooling per kilogram circulated.

A cap inside a policy that is lower than the policy's overall limit and applies to one peril or one category of loss — hail, flood, debris removal. Sublimits are where a policy that looks adequate at the headline limit turns out not to be.

The package a broker takes to market for a risk: exposure schedules, loss history, engineering reports, certifications and the narrative explaining why this account is better than its class. The quality of a submission is most of what a broker is actually selling.

The package a supplier sends after award — drawings, ratings, test reports, wiring diagrams — for the engineer of record to approve before manufacturing starts. Approval, not the purchase order, is usually what releases the factory slot.

The contractual milestone at which a building is usable for its intended purpose, even with minor work outstanding. It usually starts warranties and ends the daily damages a contractor pays for being late, so disputes over the date are common and expensive.

The fenced yard where transmission voltage is stepped down through large transformers and routed through switchgear onto distribution or onto a customer's own feeders. A data-center campus gets one — often several — and the transformer lead time, the land and the transmission line feeding it are what a utility means when it says it cannot connect a load before a given year.

One complete switching position in a substation: the breaker, the disconnects, the earthing switches, the instrument transformers and the protection belonging to a single circuit. Substations are counted, priced and extended in bays.

The layered board a processor die is mounted on inside its package, carrying the die's thousands of connections out to the pins or balls beneath. It is where the power delivery network ends — and, increasingly, where the last converter is asked to sit.

The growth of hard lead-sulphate crystals on a lead-acid plate left partly discharged. The crystals do not dissolve back on charge, so the capacity is gone for good — the dominant ageing mechanism in any lead battery that is cycled.

A device storing energy as separated electric charge rather than as a chemical reaction. It holds far less energy than a battery of the same size but takes it in and gives it back within milliseconds, over and over, for many years — which makes it the right part for absorbing a spike and the wrong one for riding out an outage.

How many degrees of extra warming the refrigerant vapour has above its boiling point when it leaves the evaporator. It is the margin that stops liquid reaching the compressor, and it is actively controlled.

A silicon MOSFET structure that buries alternating columns of opposite doping in the drift region so it can be doped harder without losing its voltage rating. It buys several times lower on-resistance for a given area than plain silicon and is what keeps silicon competitive at 600–900 volts.

Transmission a utility builds for its own reliability, ageing-equipment or local service needs rather than to solve a regional problem the grid operator identified. It enters the regional plan without the competitive window or the benefit-cost test that regional projects face, which is why consumer advocates treat it as the least-reviewed large category of utility spending.

Dependence on a small number of suppliers for a critical input. For a compute buyer it is measured in gigawatts per counterparty; the mitigation is more suppliers, which costs engineering and negotiating leverage.

A guarantee from a third party that a contractor or supplier will perform its contract, with the surety stepping in or paying if it does not. Sureties underwrite the supplier's creditworthiness before issuing, so the firms that would benefit most from one are usually the least able to obtain it.

The flow breakdown that occurs when a centrifugal compressor is asked for more pressure rise than its current flow can sustain: the gas momentarily reverses. It is noisy, damaging, and the reason a centrifugal chiller has a minimum load.

A federal rule that lets a new resource — typically a battery — use the part of an existing generator's grid connection that the generator does not use, without joining the queue from scratch. It is one of the fastest ways to add storage to an operating solar or wind site.

Insurance placed with a carrier that is not licensed (admitted) in the buyer's state, allowed for risks the admitted market will not write, through a specially licensed broker or agent. Freer on price and terms, but surplus-lines carriers do not participate in state guaranty funds.

The assemblies of breakers, switches, and protective relays that route power and isolate faults at a substation or in a power room. It is where the electrical system decides which circuits go dark when something fails — and, built into factory-tested skids, it is how much of a data center's power room now arrives on site.

What a customer must spend, in money or disruption, to move from one supplier to another — retraining, requalification, new spares, lost integration. It is the main force resisting commoditisation in equipment markets, and coupling a warranty to a long service agreement raises it deliberately.

How many times a second a switching converter turns on and off. A higher frequency lets the inductors, transformers and capacitors that smooth the output shrink in proportion, at the cost of more switching loss — the trade that wide-bandgap semiconductors and soft switching exist to improve.

Energy burned each time a transistor turns on or off, because for a few hundred nanoseconds it is carrying current and holding voltage at the same time. It scales with switching frequency, which is why a converter designer trades frequency — and therefore filter size and response speed — against efficiency.

Matching a generator's voltage, frequency, phase angle and phase rotation to a live bus before its breaker closes. Close out of step and the machine takes a torque shock and a current surge; the synchronizer or sync-check relay exists to make that impossible.

A large generator spinning in synchronism with the grid with no fuel and no turbine — it produces no energy, but supplies inertia, reactive power, and fault current on demand. Retired coal and gas units are being converted into them, keeping the machine and its interconnection alive to stabilize the grid that replaced it.

An AC machine whose rotor turns in exact step with the grid frequency — 1,500 or 1,800 rpm for a four-pole machine at 50 or 60 Hz — carrying a magnetic field set by its excitation. Driven one way it is a motor, the other way a generator; in a rotary UPS it does both, and because its output is made by a spinning magnet rather than by switching, the waveform is inherently a sine wave.
